entries.question: How did Judas die?
entries.summary: Matthew 27:5 has Judas return the silver, throw it down in the temple, and go hang himself — a tidy suicide-by-hanging. Acts 1:18 has Judas buy a field with the blood money, fall headlong in it, and burst open with his bowels gushing out — a graphic falling-apart death with no hanging mentioned. Two New Testament accounts, two completely different mechanisms of death.
entries.commentary: This is the textbook Sunday School contradiction and the apologist responses are equally textbook. The standard harmonization, run by Archer and Geisler and Howe, is to combine the accounts: Judas hanged himself, the rope or branch broke, and his body fell and ruptured. It's mechanically possible — a body left hanging in the Palestinian sun for any length of time would bloat, and a fall onto rocks could split a decomposing corpse open. The trouble is that neither text actually says that. Matthew says Judas hanged himself and stops there. Acts says he fell headlong and burst open, with no mention of a rope. You have to import the missing pieces from one account into the other to make the harmonization run. There's a bigger problem too: the *agent* of the field purchase. In Matthew the chief priests buy the potter's field with the returned silver because they can't put blood money in the treasury. In Acts Judas himself buys the field 'with the reward of iniquity.' That's a separate contradiction (the next entry covers it) but it points to the same diagnosis — these are two independent traditions about the death of Judas circulating in early Christianity, each tied to an etiology for 'the field of blood' (*Hakeldama*), and neither author knows or cares about the other's version. Raymond Brown's *Death of the Messiah* lays out both traditions side by side and concludes they're independent legends developed to explain a known place name in Jerusalem and to satisfy the theological need for Judas to die badly. The Matthean account leans on Old Testament suicide echoes (Ahithophel in 2 Sam 17:23) to make Judas a typological traitor; the Lukan account in Acts leans on graphic divine-judgment death imagery (cf. Antiochus IV in 2 Macc 9:7-12). Two evangelists writing two theological obituaries. Take your pick: harmonize with imported details neither text supplies, or accept that early Christian tradition didn't have one settled story about how Judas died.

answers.answer_explanation: Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What is that to us? see thou to that. And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself. And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in. Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value; And gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me. Matthew 27:3-10

Now this man [Judas] purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out. And it was known unto all the dwellers at Jerusalem; insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood. Acts 1:18-19

commentary_out.commentary:
The two New Testament notices of Judas's death describe incompatible mechanisms. Matthew 27:5 reports that Judas, seized with remorse, returned the silver, flung it into the temple, departed, and 'hanged himself' (apēnxato, the same verb used in the Septuagint of Ahithophel's suicide in 2 Samuel 17:23). Acts 1:18 reports that 'falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out' (prēnēs genomenos elakēsen mesos kai exechythē panta ta splanchna autou). Matthew gives a hanging and no fall; Acts gives a fall and rupture with no rope.

The classic harmonization, defended by Gleason Archer and by Norman Geisler and Thomas Howe in When Critics Ask, combines the two: Judas hanged himself, the rope or branch later gave way, and the bloated corpse fell and split open on the rocks below. The medical plausibility is real — a body left hanging in a warm climate undergoes putrefaction and gas accumulation within days, and a fall onto rough ground could rupture the distended abdominal wall. The steel-man here is that the two reports are partial, each preserving a phase of a single event. The objection is textual rather than physiological: neither author writes the composite. Matthew narrates a completed suicide and moves on to the priests; nothing in his text anticipates a later fall. Acts narrates a fall and rupture as the death itself and gives no hint of a prior hanging. To run the harmonization one must import the rope into Acts and the fall into Matthew, supplying from each text precisely the element the other omits. The Greek prēnēs genomenos ('falling headlong / face-forward,' or on a minority lexical reading 'swelling up') reads as the cause of death, not as the post-mortem sequel to a hanging.

The accounts also diverge on the agent of the field's purchase and on why it is called the field of blood — a related contradiction treated separately — which signals that these are not two halves of one report but two independent traditions, each an etiology for the Jerusalem place name Hakeldama. Raymond Brown's Death of the Messiah sets the traditions side by side and concludes they developed independently to explain a known field and to satisfy the theological expectation that the betrayer meet a fitting end. The two obituaries are theologically shaped in different directions. Matthew models Judas on the archetypal traitor Ahithophel, David's counselor who betrayed him and then hanged himself (2 Sam 17:23), reinforcing the typology of treachery within the inner circle. Acts deploys the genre of the gruesome divine-judgment death, whose closest scriptural and intertestamental analogues are the bowel-bursting ends of Antiochus IV in 2 Maccabees 9:7-12 and of Herod Agrippa I in Acts 12:23 (eaten of worms) — the wicked persecutor undone from within. A third early tradition, preserved by Papias (in Apollinaris's quotation), has Judas swell to monstrous size and die crushed in his own bulk, neither cleanly hanged nor cleanly fallen, confirming that the early church carried multiple incompatible accounts.

The fork is therefore stark. The harmonizer must graft details across two texts that each present a self-sufficient and different mode of death, against the grain of the Greek of Acts 1:18; or one accepts that primitive Christianity had no single settled account of how Judas died, only the shared conviction that he died badly and that a Jerusalem field bore the name 'of blood.' Verdict: genuine contradiction reflecting two independent etiological traditions.
commentary_out.change_summary: Deepened the Judas-death commentary with the Greek of Acts 1:18, the medical plausibility and its limits, the Ahithophel and Antiochus typological backgrounds, the Papias variant tradition, and tighter framing of the dual etiology.

issues.problem: The commentary attributes the Judas-swells-and-bursts variant to 'Papias (in Apollinaris's quotation).' The standard attribution is that the Papias fragment on Judas's death is preserved in a scholion/catena attributed to Apollinaris of Laodicea. The framing is essentially correct, but stating it as a clean 'Papias (in Apollinaris's quotation)' overstates certainty: the Apollinarian attribution and the exact wording are themselves debated in the scholarship (e.g., the fragment survives in catenae; the connection to Apollinaris is the conventional but not uncontested route of transmission).
issues.correction: Soften to: 'a fragment of Papias preserved in later catena material (conventionally traced through Apollinaris of Laodicea),' acknowledging the transmission is via catena fragments rather than a secure direct quotation.

issues.problem: The commentary glosses prēnēs genomenos as possibly meaning 'swelling up' on 'a minority lexical reading.' This reflects a genuine but contested proposal (the suggestion that prēnēs relates to prēthō, 'to swell,' harmonizing Acts with the Papias tradition). Presenting it as a recognized 'minority lexical reading' is fair, though it is a fairly fringe emendation/etymology rather than a standard lexical sense.
issues.correction: Optionally note that the 'swelling' sense rests on a proposed connection to a different root and is not the standard meaning of prēnēs ('headlong, prone'); no correction to the main argument required.

entries.question: Did both thieves revile Jesus?
entries.summary: Mark 15:32 says both of those crucified with Jesus reviled him. Matthew 27:44 says the thieves (plural) cast the same in his teeth. Luke 23:39-43 splits them apart: one malefactor rails on Jesus while the *other* rebukes him, defends Jesus' innocence, and is promised paradise. So Mark and Matthew have both criminals mocking; Luke has one mocking and one converting.
entries.commentary: The standard apologist harmonization, run by Archer, Wenham, and Blomberg, is that *both* criminals initially mocked Jesus (Mark and Matthew capture this early moment) but then *one* of them had a change of heart partway through the crucifixion and became the penitent thief (Luke captures this later moment). It's chronologically possible — crucifixion lasted hours, and someone in agony watching another dying man behave with dignity might plausibly soften his attitude. So the harmonization gets some credit for being mechanically coherent. The trouble is the *function* of the penitent thief in Luke's theology. Luke is the gospel of repentance and the gospel of the marginalized — the good thief is the climactic example of last-minute forgiveness, a structural parallel to the prodigal son and the tax collector. Luke also redacts the cry of dereliction *out* of his crucifixion scene and replaces it with the calm 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.' Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Luke and Bart Ehrman in *Jesus, Interrupted* both argue Luke is reshaping the entire crucifixion theologically: Mark's anguished, abandoned Jesus becomes Luke's serene, forgiveness-dispensing Jesus, and the penitent thief is part of that reshaping. The thief isn't a historical detail Luke added — he's a theological figure Luke needed. Steel-manning the harmonization: yes, the 'one thief changed his mind' reconstruction is internally consistent. And ancient Greek can use plural for generic groups even when only one member acts. But Mark and Matthew don't hint at a conversion, and Luke doesn't hint at an initial mockery from his good thief. Each evangelist tells a complete and self-consistent story. The harmonized story is one no evangelist tells. Take your pick: redactional theology or the imported composite.

answers.answer_explanation:
And they that were crucified with him reviled him. Mark 15:32

The thieves also, which were crucified with him, cast the same in his teeth. Matthew 27:44

And one of the malefactors which were hanged railed on him, saying, If thou be Christ, save thyself and us. But the other answering rebuked him, saying, Dost not thou fear God, seeing thou art in the same condemnation? And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss. And he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. Luke 23:39-42

commentary_out.commentary:
Mark 15:32 states flatly that 'they that were crucified with him reviled him' — both of them. Matthew 27:44, following Mark, has 'the thieves' (plural) cast the same insults in his teeth. Luke 23:39-43 tells a different story: one criminal rails at Jesus ('If thou be Christ, save thyself and us'), while the other rebukes the first, affirms Jesus' innocence ('this man hath done nothing amiss'), and asks to be remembered in Jesus' kingdom, receiving the promise, 'Today shalt thou be with me in paradise.' Mark and Matthew have two mockers; Luke has one mocker and one penitent.

The standard harmonization, argued by Gleason Archer, John Wenham, and Craig Blomberg, is chronological: both criminals mocked Jesus at first (the moment Mark and Matthew preserve), and one of them later underwent a change of heart and became the penitent thief Luke records. Crucifixion was a slow death lasting hours, and the proposal that a dying man, watching Jesus' bearing, came to repentance over time is psychologically plausible and internally consistent. A second, weaker supporting move notes that Greek (like English) can use a plural loosely for a group when strictly only part of the group acts — 'they reviled him' could be a generalizing plural. These observations earn the harmonization a hearing.

But the harmonization founders on the wider evidence of Luke's redactional program, which the conversion theory does not merely supplement but contradicts in spirit. Luke systematically reshapes Mark's crucifixion. He removes the cry of dereliction — Mark's 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me' (Mark 15:34) is absent from Luke — and replaces the Markan portrait of an anguished, forsaken Jesus with a serene, sovereign one who prays 'Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do' (23:34) and dies committing his spirit calmly to the Father (23:46). Within this thoroughgoing recasting, the penitent thief is not an isolated extra fact but an integral element: he is the climactic instance of Luke's signature theme of last-minute repentance and the embrace of the outcast, of a piece with the prodigal son (Luke 15), the tax collector justified over the Pharisee (18:9-14), and Zacchaeus (19:1-10). Joseph Fitzmyer in the Anchor Bible Luke reads the scene as Lukan composition serving these theological ends, and Bart Ehrman in *Jesus, Interrupted* uses it as a paradigm case of how Luke transforms Mark's dying Jesus into a model of forgiveness. The good thief, on this reading, is a figure Luke's theology requires, not a memory Luke alone retained.

The decisive point against the conversion harmonization is narrative: no Gospel actually tells the two-stage story. Mark and Matthew give no hint of any subsequent softening — for them the mockery from both sides is part of the total abandonment of Jesus, joined by passersby and chief priests. Luke gives no hint that his penitent thief ever mocked; from his first words the man fears God and defends Jesus. The reconstruction in which both first revile and then one repents is a composite reverse-engineered to reconcile the texts, narrated by none of them. The generic-plural defense is also strained: Mark's and Matthew's plural is most naturally read as genuinely dual, paralleling the dual mockery from rulers, soldiers, and crowd that frames the scene, and Matthew has independently chosen to retain and even underscore Mark's 'both.'

The most economical explanation is redaction: Luke has rewritten the shared Markan datum of dual mockery to create the penitent thief, in service of his distinctive theology of forgiveness. The differing accounts cannot both be straightforwardly historical without importing a sequence neither narrates.

Verdict: genuine contradiction at the narrative level; best explained as Lukan redaction rather than a single harmonizable sequence.

The commentary itself grants the chronological 'one thief changed his mind' reconstruction is 'internally consistent' and 'psychologically plausible,' and this is a standard, defensible harmonization accepted by many. entries.question: Did Mary Magdalene recognize Jesus when he first appeared to her?
entries.summary: Matthew 28:9 has Mary and the other Mary meet the risen Jesus, grab his feet, and worship him — no confusion, instant recognition. John 20:14 has Mary Magdalene look right at him and not realize who he is, mistaking him for the gardener. Luke 24:23 throws a third curve: in Luke's version Mary doesn't see Jesus at the tomb at all, only a vision of angels. Three Gospels, three incompatible accounts of the same moment.
entries.commentary: The contradiction sits right at the foundational event of Christianity, and the harmonizers know it, which is why the apologist playbook here is so creative. Gleason Archer (Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, Zondervan 1982, pp. 347-349) and Norman Geisler argue these are sequential encounters — first Jesus blocks Mary from recognizing him in John, then later in Matthew she sees him clearly with the other Mary. The problem is that this requires reading the texts as a single composite narrative the evangelists themselves never wrote. Matthew has the women, plural, meet Jesus on the way back from the tomb after seeing the angel. John has Mary alone, returning a second time after fetching Peter and the Beloved Disciple. These are not two scenes you can stack on top of each other without rewriting both. And Luke is even worse for the harmonizer — in Luke 24:22-24 the women report seeing angels who said Jesus was alive, not Jesus himself, and the men later go check the tomb and find it empty without anyone meeting the risen Christ there. That is of course Luke's editorial choice, but it directly contradicts both Matthew and John on whether Jesus appeared at the tomb at all. The critical consensus, from Raymond Brown forward, is that each evangelist is shaping the resurrection appearances to serve his own theological program — Matthew's high Christology demands immediate worship, John's stresses recognition through hearing the Shepherd's voice, Luke's emphasizes the witness of angels and the disciples' slowness to believe. The differences are not chronological gaps the reader is supposed to fill in; they are the data.

commentary_out.commentary:
At the foundational moment of the resurrection narratives the three gospels diverge on whether and how Mary Magdalene encountered the risen Jesus. Matthew 28:9 has Jesus meet the women (plural) as they leave the tomb; they 'took hold of his feet and worshiped him' (*ekratēsan autou tous podas*) — instant, unhesitating recognition and homage. John 20:14-15 has Mary alone, who 'turned around and saw Jesus standing there, but did not know that it was Jesus,' mistaking him for the gardener until he speaks her name. Luke 24:22-24 has no tomb appearance of Jesus at all: the women report only 'a vision of angels who said he was alive,' and when the disciples verify the tomb they find it empty but meet no risen Christ there.

The apologetic harmonization, advanced by Gleason Archer and by Norman Geisler and Thomas Howe, reads these as sequential moments: Jesus first appears to Mary while withholding recognition (John), then later appears to the group with recognition granted (Matthew). The strongest form notes that John 20 does narrate a delayed recognition resolved when Jesus says 'Mary' (John 20:16), so non-recognition followed by recognition is internal to John and not implausible in principle. But stacking John's scene under Matthew's requires rewriting both. Matthew has the women, plural, meet Jesus on the road back from the tomb immediately after the angel; John has Mary, singular, encountering him only after she has run to fetch Peter and the Beloved Disciple and returned a second time (John 20:2, 11). The casts, the locations relative to the errand, and the choreography differ. There is a further unresolved snag the two-stage reading creates: in Matthew the women clasp his feet, whereas John's Jesus tells Mary 'do not cling to me' (*mē mou haptou*, John 20:17) — the Matthean foot-holding and the Johannine prohibition pull against each other if they are the same woman in adjacent moments.

Luke is the harder problem for any sequential reconstruction. Luke 24:22-24 does not merely omit a tomb appearance; it positively reports that the women saw angels rather than Jesus, and that those who checked the tomb 'did not see him.' Luke reserves the first dominical appearances for the Emmaus road and the upper room (Luke 24:13-49), a deliberate editorial structure that builds his theme of disciples 'slow of heart to believe' (24:25). To harmonize, one must treat Luke's silence as mere omission, but Luke 24:24's 'him they did not see' is an assertion, not a gap.

The critical reading, from Raymond Brown forward, is that each evangelist shapes the appearance to his own theology. Matthew's high Christology produces immediate *proskynēsis*, worship, consistent with his framing of the angel-theophany earlier in the chapter. John's recognition-by-voice enacts the Good Shepherd motif of John 10:3-4, 'the sheep hear his voice … he calls his own by name' — Mary knows him not by sight but when he names her, a theological point requiring the initial non-recognition. Luke foregrounds angelic testimony and the disciples' incredulity, deferring recognition to the breaking of bread at Emmaus (24:30-31), itself a eucharistic motif. Dale Allison catalogues these as variant traditions each evangelist has developed rather than complementary slices of one sequence, and Bart Ehrman uses precisely this cluster to illustrate that the differences are the data, not gaps for the harmonizer to bridge. Verdict: genuine contradiction; the two-stage appearance can be stipulated only by overriding Matthew's plural witnesses, John's choreography and *mē mou haptou*, and Luke's explicit denial that anyone saw Jesus at the tomb.

entries.question: What did Jesus do after his baptism?
entries.summary: Mark 1:12-13 says the Spirit immediately drove Jesus into the wilderness for forty days of temptation right after his baptism. John 1:35-2:1 has Jesus on day two calling disciples and on day three attending a wedding at Cana — no wilderness, no forty-day fast, no satanic temptation. Same Jesus, same post-baptism window, two incompatible itineraries.
entries.commentary: The contradiction is sharp because Mark uses the Greek word euthus — 'immediately' — to mark the temporal sequence. Mark 1:12 literally says 'and immediately the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.' No gap allowed. John's narrative, by contrast, gives a day-by-day chronology that places Jesus among John the Baptist's followers the day after the baptism, then in Galilee gathering disciples, then at a wedding in Cana on day three. Forty days of solitary fasting cannot fit anywhere in John's chronology. The standard harmonization, found in D. A. Carson's PNTC commentary on John (Eerdmans 1991, pp. 146-149) and earlier in Leon Morris, is to insert the forty-day temptation before John 1:35 — claiming John picks up the narrative after the wilderness episode is already over. This requires the baptism itself to have happened before John 1:19, somewhere off-page, and Jesus to have spent forty days in the wilderness between that off-page baptism and the day John 1 actually starts recounting. The text gives no hint of any of this. John 1:32-34 has the Baptist describing the descent of the Spirit at Jesus' baptism as if it just happened, then on 'the next day' (1:35) Jesus walks past with disciples in tow. There is no forty-day gap to be found unless you invent one. The simpler reading is that John's Gospel preserves a different and independent tradition about Jesus' early ministry that knows nothing of the wilderness temptation. That is the consensus reading from Raymond Brown through Bart Ehrman. Mark's wilderness account itself has clear theological function — Jesus as the new Israel re-tested for forty (years/days) in the desert — and the Synoptic versions in Matthew and Luke elaborate it heavily. John dropped the scene because it didn't serve his theological program of the cosmic Logos who needs no testing. Two early traditions, two Christologies, one impossible composite.

commentary_out.commentary:
Mark and John give incompatible accounts of what Jesus did in the days immediately after his baptism. Mark 1:12-13 reports that "immediately the spirit driveth him into the wilderness," where he remained "forty days, tempted of Satan." The temporal marker is the characteristically Markan εὐθύς, "immediately" — the word recurs dozens of times in the Gospel and here forecloses any gap between baptism and wilderness. John, by contrast, supplies a tight day-by-day chronology: the Baptist testifies to the Spirit's descent (John 1:32-34); "the next day" Jesus passes by and disciples begin to follow (1:35-37); "the day following" he goes into Galilee and calls Philip (1:43); and "the third day" he is at the wedding in Cana (2:1). Across roughly the first week after the baptism testimony, John has Jesus gathering followers and attending a celebration — no solitude, no fast, no satanic test. Forty days of wilderness withdrawal cannot be inserted anywhere into that sequence.

The strongest harmonization, found in Leon Morris and D. A. Carson, places the forty-day temptation before John 1:35: John, on this reading, narrates events after the wilderness episode is already complete, so the baptism itself occurred off-page before John 1:19 and the temptation in the unrecorded interval. Steel-manned, the proposal exploits a genuine feature of the Fourth Gospel — John never directly narrates the baptism at all, but only the Baptist's retrospective testimony to it (1:32-34), which leaves room to argue that time has elapsed. John also omits much that the Synoptics include, so omission of the temptation would be unremarkable in itself.

The difficulty is the texture of John 1 itself. The Baptist's words in 1:32-34 ("I saw the Spirit descending... and I knew him not") read as fresh testimony to a recent event, and the "next day" of 1:35 follows immediately upon that testimony, not upon some forty-day absence. To make room for the temptation, the harmonizer must posit that between the Spirit's descent and the Baptist's report of it, Jesus had already vanished into the desert for forty days and returned — yet John 1:29-36 presents the Baptist pointing to Jesus as present and walking nearby ("Behold the Lamb of God," 1:29, 36), not as someone six weeks gone. The forty-day gap is not found in the text; it is imported to protect the Synoptic timeline.

The critical reading, represented by Raymond Brown, Joel Marcus, and Bart Ehrman, is that John preserves an independent tradition of Jesus' early activity that simply does not include the wilderness temptation. The reason is theological as much as historical. Mark's wilderness scene is freighted with Israel-typology — Jesus driven into the desert, tested forty days as Israel was tested forty years, ministered to by angels — and Matthew and Luke expand it into a structured three-fold dialogue with Satan keyed to Deuteronomy. John's Christology has no place for such testing: his Jesus is the pre-existent Logos (1:1-14) who possesses the Spirit "without measure" (3:34) and is never shown in doubt, struggle, or temptation; even Gethsemane is recast. As Marcus notes of Mark and Brown of John, the two evangelists are pursuing different portraits, and the wilderness episode belongs to one program and is alien to the other. The result is two genuinely incompatible itineraries for the same window of time, each shaped by its author's theology. Verdict: genuine contradiction reflecting independent traditions and divergent Christologies.

entries.question: Did the cock crow before or after Peter's denial?
entries.summary: Matthew 26:74, Luke 22:60, and John 18:27 all have the cock crow after Peter's third denial. Mark 14:67-72 has the cock crow after the first denial and then a second time after the third — and Jesus' prediction in Mark 14:30 specifies 'before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice.' Three Gospels have one cock-crow at the end of the sequence; Mark has two, with the first happening after denial number one.
entries.commentary: The contradiction sits between Mark and the rest of the synoptic tradition. Mark 14:30 has Jesus predict 'before the cock crow twice' — a two-crow sequence. Matthew, Luke, and John all flatten this to a single crow at the end. The Markan account is internally consistent: the cock crows after denial one (Mark 14:68 in the Majority Text and TR, though this verse is missing from some early manuscripts including Sinaiticus), and again after denial three (Mark 14:72), matching the 'crow twice' prediction in Mark 14:30. The other Gospels appear to have edited Mark to simplify the prediction and the fulfillment. The standard apologetic move, defended by Gleason Archer (Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, Zondervan 1982, pp. 343-345) and earlier by John Wenham, is to argue Mark preserves the more detailed account and the others abbreviate. That is technically a non-contradiction defense: if Mark is more detailed and the others omit the first crow without denying it, no formal contradiction obtains. The weakness of this defense is that Jesus' prediction itself differs across the Gospels — Matthew 26:34 and Luke 22:34 have him predict a single crow ('before the cock crow') while Mark 14:30 has him predict two ('before the cock crow twice'). Jesus cannot have predicted both. One evangelist is preserving the original logion and the others have changed it, or vice versa. The textual situation is also messy — Mark 14:68's reference to the first crow is missing from some manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus), which Bruce Metzger argues is the original Markan text and the addition is a later scribal harmonization. If Metzger is right, even Mark originally had only one crow, and the doubled crow in the textus receptus is itself a harmonizing intrusion. Either way, the predictions don't match across the Gospels. That is the underlying contradiction the harmonizers cannot escape.

commentary_out.commentary:
The contradiction operates on two levels: the prediction Jesus makes and the fulfillment that follows. At the prediction level, Mark 14:30 has Jesus say "before the cock crow twice, you will deny me three times" (prin ē dis alektora phōnēsai), while Matthew 26:34 and Luke 22:34 have him predict a single crow: "before the cock crows" (prin alektora phōnēsai). John 13:38 likewise has a single crow. These are not two descriptions of one event but two different prophecies placed on Jesus' lips. He cannot have said both "before the cock crows twice" and "before the cock crows"; one form is original and the others have been altered. The Markan "twice" is the harder, more specific reading and is unlikely to have been invented; the Synoptic parallels look like simplifications of it.

At the fulfillment level the picture is the same. Matthew 26:74, Luke 22:60, and John 18:27 record a single cock-crow after the third denial. Mark 14:68 (in the Majority Text and the Textus Receptus) reports a first crow after the initial denial, and Mark 14:72 a second crow after the third, matching the doubled prediction. Mark's account is internally consistent; the other three are internally consistent with their own single-crow predictions. The problem is cross-Gospel: the traditions diverge on how Jesus' words ran and how they were fulfilled.

The textual evidence complicates Mark itself. The clause kai alektōr ephōnēsen ("and the cock crew") at the end of Mark 14:68 is absent from Sinaiticus (a), B (Vaticanus), L, W, and other significant witnesses, and the word dis ("twice") in 14:72 and 14:30 is likewise unstable across the tradition. Bruce Metzger's textual commentary (1994, pp. 95-97) judges that the first-crow notice in 14:68 and the "twice" wording are likely secondary scribal harmonizations designed to make the narration line up with the prediction — meaning even Mark may originally have had only a single crow, with the doubled version a later intrusion. Joel Marcus (2009, pp. 998-1015) and the editors of NA28 weigh the same data; the matter is genuinely disputed at the textual level, but on every reconstruction the predictions across the four Gospels do not agree.

The standard harmonization, advanced by Gleason Archer (1982, pp. 343-345) and John Wenham (1992, pp. 73-78), is that Mark simply preserves a fuller account: the others mention only the second, decisive crow without denying the first, so no formal contradiction obtains in the narration. As far as the fulfillment goes, this is a coherent more-detail/less-detail argument and would carry weight if the only difference were the number of crows narrated. But it cannot reach the prediction. "Before the cock crow twice" and "before the cock crow" are mutually exclusive accounts of what Jesus actually said, and the harmonization offers no mechanism to make both true. Davies and Allison (1997, pp. 540-551) and Raymond Brown (1994, pp. 605-626) treat the divergence as a clear instance of Matthew and Luke editing their Markan source — flattening the distinctive double-crow into the single crow that fit the proverbial "cockcrow" as a marker of dawn.

Verdict: genuine contradiction at the level of Jesus' prediction, compounded by an unstable Markan text; the more-detail harmonization addresses only the narration, not the differing prophecies.

entries.question: When was the blind man (or men) healed?
entries.summary: Matthew 20:29-30 and Mark 10:46 say Jesus healed blind men as he was departing Jericho. Luke 18:35 says Jesus healed a blind man as he approached Jericho. Matthew has two blind men, Mark and Luke have one. The three Synoptic gospels disagree on both the number of those healed and the geographic timing of the miracle.
entries.commentary:
This is a textbook Synoptic Problem case. Mark 10:46 has one blind man, Bartimaeus son of Timaeus, healed as Jesus leaves Jericho. Matthew 20:29-30 keeps the post-Jericho timing but turns one blind man into two and drops the name. Luke 18:35 keeps a single anonymous blind man but moves the healing to before Jericho — "as he was come nigh unto Jericho."

The standard apologetic harmonization runs along two tracks. Gleason Archer argues that there were actually three blind men — one Jesus encountered approaching Jericho (Luke), and two more on the way out (Matthew/Mark) — and the gospels each report partial overlapping incidents. Craig Blomberg offers a variant where Luke is describing Jesus entering the new Roman Jericho while Matthew and Mark describe him leaving the old Jewish Jericho a mile away. Both are clever and both are ad-hoc.

The Synoptic Problem solution from Joel Marcus, Ulrich Luz, and the broader two-source-hypothesis consensus is much simpler. Mark wrote first with one named blind man at the exit from Jericho. Matthew, working from Mark, doubled the figure — Matthew has a recurring pattern of doubling Mark's figures (compare Matthew 8:28's two demoniacs against Mark 5:2's one). Luke, also working from Mark, kept the single blind man but relocated the scene from the exit to the entrance because Luke 19:1-10 immediately follows with the Zacchaeus story inside Jericho — Luke needed Jesus to enter Jericho after the healing, so he moved the healing to before the entrance.

Luz's Hermeneia commentary on Matthew documents the doubling pattern, and Marcus's Mark commentary lays out the priority of Mark's account. The harmonizations require either an implausible three-blind-men coincidence or a geographic shell game involving twin Jerichos. The redactional explanation is dramatically more parsimonious: each evangelist adjusted the Markan scene for their own narrative purposes.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is a textbook Synoptic-Problem case in which the simplest explanation is editorial, not historical. On the two-source hypothesis, Mark is the earliest of the three accounts. Mark 10:46-52 narrates a single named beggar, Bartimaeus son of Timaeus, healed "as he went out of Jericho." Matthew 20:29-34 keeps Mark's post-Jericho setting ("as they departed from Jericho") but reports two blind men and drops the Aramaic name. Luke 18:35-43 keeps Mark's single anonymous beggar but moves the scene to before the city: "as he was come nigh unto Jericho." So the three accounts diverge on both the number healed (one vs. two) and the geography (entering vs. leaving).

The two leading harmonizations are ingenious but ad hoc. Gleason Archer proposes three blind men in two separate encounters — one as Jesus approached (Luke), two as he left (Matthew/Mark) — with each evangelist reporting a partial slice. The difficulty is that all three narrate what reads as the same single episode, with the same cry ("thou son of David, have mercy"), the same roadside setting, and the same healing, and none signals a separate occasion. Craig Blomberg's alternative invokes archaeology: Herodian Jericho lay roughly a mile from the old Jewish/Tell es-Sultan site, so Jesus could be "leaving" one Jericho while "approaching" the other, with the healing in between. This is geographically real — there were indeed two adjacent Jerichos — but the gospels show no awareness of a two-city distinction, and the move still leaves the number discrepancy (one vs. two) untouched.

The redactional account is far more economical and explains both divergences at once. First, the number: Matthew demonstrably has a habit of doubling Markan figures. He turns Mark's single Gerasene demoniac (Mark 5:2) into two (Matthew 8:28), and in the very next pericope after this one he reads Zechariah 9:9 to produce two animals at the triumphal entry (Matthew 21:2-7) where Mark has one colt (Mark 11:2). The doubling of one blind man into two fits this established Matthean tendency. Second, the geography: Luke relocates the healing because of what he places immediately after it. Luke 19:1-10 narrates Zacchaeus *inside* Jericho; for that scene to follow, Jesus must still be entering the city when the blind man is healed, so Luke shifts the cure to the approach. Luz's Hermeneia commentary documents the Matthean doubling pattern, and Marcus's Anchor Yale commentary establishes Markan priority and Mark's place as the source both later evangelists redacted.

The harmonizations require either an unlikely three-beggar coincidence or a twin-Jericho shell game that still cannot account for the doubled number. The redactional explanation accounts for every difference — number and direction — from known compositional habits of Matthew and Luke working on a shared Markan source. Verdict: genuine contradiction at the narrative level, best explained as Synoptic redaction of a single Markan story.

entries.question: Did Jesus go to heaven after he died but before his ascension?
entries.summary: Luke 23:43 has Jesus promise the criminal on the cross, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." John 20:17 has the resurrected Jesus tell Mary Magdalene, "Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father." The Lukan promise puts Jesus in paradise the day of his death; the Johannine statement keeps him from ascending until after the resurrection.
entries.commentary:
This is a clean contradiction at the surface, and the harmonizations require theological footwork. Luke 23:43 has Jesus and the repentant criminal in paradise on the day of the crucifixion — Friday. John 20:17, set on Easter Sunday or shortly after, has Jesus telling Mary not to touch him because he hasn't yet ascended to the Father.

The most common harmonization, developed across the patristic tradition and adopted by modern apologists like Norman Geisler, is that "paradise" and "the Father" are different locations. Paradise in this scheme is an intermediate state — sometimes identified with the "Abraham's bosom" of Luke 16:22, sometimes with the "prison" Christ preaches to in 1 Peter 3:19 — distinct from the heavenly throne room of the Father. Jesus could be in paradise Friday and still not have ascended to the Father by Sunday morning. That harmonization has internal logic but it's reading a complex eschatological geography into texts that don't develop one.

Another apologetic move, going back to the Greek punctuation problem, repositions the comma in Luke 23:43: "Verily I say unto thee today, shalt thou be with me in paradise." That reading saves Jesus from being in paradise Friday by making "today" modify the speech-act rather than the destination. The problem is that this is a violation of Luke's standard phrasing — Luke uses "verily I say unto thee" or "verily I say unto you" 27 times without ever pairing it with a redundant "today." The repositioned-comma reading is grammatically possible but stylistically alien to Luke.

Fitzmyer takes Luke 23:43 at its surface meaning: Jesus tells the criminal he will be with him in paradise that very day. Brown's treatment in the Death of the Messiah agrees. The most economical reading is that Luke and John have different and incompatible post-mortem itineraries for Jesus — Luke's is paradise-then-resurrection-then-ascension, John's is somewhere-not-the-Father-yet until after the resurrection. The harmonizations need to import categories not in the texts.

commentary_out.commentary:
On the surface this is a clean contradiction, and every proposed reconciliation requires importing categories the texts do not themselves supply. Luke 23:43 has Jesus promise the penitent criminal, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" — locating both in paradeisos on the day of the crucifixion (Friday). John 20:17, set on Easter morning, has the risen Jesus tell Mary Magdalene, "Touch me not [mē mou haptou]; for I am not yet ascended to my Father." If "paradise" and "the Father" name the same destination, the two statements collide: Jesus is already there Friday in Luke, not yet there Sunday in John.

The most serious harmonization, with deep patristic roots and adopted by modern apologists such as Norman Geisler, distinguishes the destinations. "Paradise" in this scheme is an intermediate abode of the righteous dead — frequently identified with the "Abraham's bosom" of Luke 16:22-23 and connected to the realm where 1 Peter 3:19 has Christ preach "to the spirits in prison" — distinct from the heavenly throne room of the Father to which the ascension (John 20:17; Acts 1:9-11) leads. On this reading Jesus could be in the intermediate paradise Friday and still not have ascended to the Father by Sunday. The view has internal coherence and real second-Temple precedent: paradeisos (a Persian loanword for a walled garden, used in the LXX for Eden) does denote an abode of the blessed in texts like 1 Enoch and the Testament of Levi, and the geography of the afterlife in early Judaism was genuinely layered. This is why the entry is best rated disputed rather than flatly unresolved: the distinction is not invented out of nothing.

But it is not in Luke or John either. Luke does not present paradise as a way-station preceding ascension; Acts 1 simply has Jesus ascend after the resurrection appearances, with no intervening cosmology mapped. The harmonization reads a multi-tiered itinerary into texts that do not develop one, and it must coordinate Luke, John, 1 Peter, and intertestamental sources into a synthetic scheme none of the authors states.

A second, weaker apologetic move repunctuates Luke 23:43 — since the earliest manuscripts lack punctuation — to read "Verily I say unto thee today, shalt thou be with me in paradise," making "today" modify the act of speaking rather than the arrival. Grammatically the comma can fall either way, but the move is stylistically alien to Luke: his fixed introductory formula is amēn legō soi/hymin ("verily I say unto thee/you"), which appears repeatedly across the Gospel as a self-contained unit and never elsewhere takes an appended "today." Inserting sēmeron into the formula is unparalleled in Lukan usage, whereas "today" attaches naturally and emphatically to the promise (Luke is fond of sēmeron — see 2:11, 4:21, 19:9). The repositioned comma solves the problem only by rewriting Luke's idiom.

Fitzmyer reads Luke 23:43 at face value — the criminal will be with Jesus in paradise that very day — and Brown concurs in *The Death of the Messiah*. Brown's John commentary, meanwhile, treats John 20:17's "not yet ascended" as integral to John's distinctive theology of glorification, in which cross, resurrection, and ascension form a unified movement to the Father not yet complete on Easter morning. The two evangelists are working out different post-mortem itineraries, and reconciling them requires a harmonizing cosmology external to both. Verdict: a real tension; harmonizable only by importing an intermediate-state scheme the texts do not articulate — hence disputed.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Defenders harmonize by distinguishing destinations — "paradise" as an intermediate state distinct from ascension "to the Father" — so that Jesus could be in paradise on Friday yet not have ascended by Easter morning. The reading has internal logic and patristic pedigree but imports an eschatological geography neither text develops; the harmonization is contested, not decisively established or refuted, hence disputed.

entries.question: Where did Jesus go when he died?
entries.summary: Luke 23:43 has Jesus promise the repentant criminal that they will be together in paradise that very day, implying Jesus went to paradise. The Apostles' Creed has Jesus descend into hell, a tradition grounded in 1 Peter 3:18-20 and 1 Peter 4:6. The biblical and creedal traditions point in opposite directions on where Jesus went between Friday and Sunday.
entries.commentary:
This is contradiction id=510 viewed from a different angle, with the added wrinkle that the "hell" answer leads with the Apostles' Creed rather than scripture. The Apostles' Creed is a fourth-century-or-later confessional document, not biblical text. The actual biblical basis for the descent-into-hell tradition is 1 Peter 3:18-20 ("by which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison") and 1 Peter 4:6 ("the gospel preached also to them that are dead"), now added to this answer's references so the contradiction rests on scripture and not just the creedal summary.

With those passages added, the contradiction is real but narrower than "heaven versus hell" suggests. The Greek of 1 Peter 3:19 doesn't use the word for hell (hades or geenna) — it says "prison" (phylake), and the spirits there are usually identified, following the Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 traditions, with the disobedient angels of Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch. So Jesus going to the "prison of the spirits" is a specifically apocalyptic-Jewish geography rather than the medieval Christian hell.

Luke 23:43's paradise (paradeisos) is also a specifically apocalyptic-Jewish term — used in 2 Corinthians 12:4 and Revelation 2:7 for the heavenly garden, and in Second Temple texts like 1 Enoch 60:8 and 2 Enoch 8 for the dwelling of the righteous dead.

So at the technical level, Luke's Jesus goes to the heavenly paradise of the righteous, while 1 Peter's Jesus goes to the prison of the disobedient spirits. Both could in principle be true on a complex post-mortem itinerary — Augustine and Aquinas worked out elaborate schemes where Jesus visited multiple post-mortem locations — but the texts themselves don't develop such a scheme. They're two independent traditions about what Jesus did between his death and resurrection.

The critical-scholarly read is that 1 Peter is using a Jewish apocalyptic tradition (the descent to the Watchers) to give Jesus' death cosmic significance, while Luke is using a different apocalyptic tradition (paradise as righteous reward) to highlight individual salvation through the cross. The Apostles' Creed pulls 1 Peter into its summary and creates the "descended into hell" formulation that medieval Latin Christianity then elaborated. This contradiction is real but the SAB framing obscures more than it reveals.

commentary_out.commentary:
The contradiction is genuine but the SAB framing — 'heaven' versus 'hell' — imports later categories that obscure what the texts actually say. The first complication is that the 'hell' answer originally led with the Apostles' Creed, a confessional summary, not Scripture. The descensus clause ('he descended into hell,' descendit ad inferna/inferos) is absent from the earliest forms of the Old Roman Creed; it appears in the fourth-century Aquileian form attested by Rufinus (c. 404) and only later becomes standard in the received Western text. The biblical substrate for the descent tradition is 1 Peter 3:18-20 ('he went and preached unto the spirits in prison') and 1 Peter 4:6 ('the gospel preached also to them that are dead'), which now ground the contradiction in Scripture rather than in a creedal paraphrase.

Once those passages carry the weight, the destinations are narrower and stranger than 'hell.' The Greek of 1 Peter 3:19 does not use hades or geenna; it says the spirits are en phylake — 'in prison.' The standard critical identification, following the trajectory of 1 Enoch and shared by Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4, is that these 'spirits in prison' are the disobedient angels (the 'sons of God' of Genesis 6:1-4, the Watchers) who were bound for their transgression before the Flood — note that 3:20 specifies they were disobedient 'in the days of Noah.' Jesus' proclamation to them is thus set in a specifically Jewish-apocalyptic cosmology of imprisoned rebel spirits, not the punitive hell of medieval Christianity. Achtemeier and Elliott both read 3:19 against this Enochic background; whether the 'preaching' is a proclamation of triumph or an offer of salvation is debated, but the locale is the Watchers' prison.

Luke's destination is equally technical. Paradeisos is a Persian loanword (pairidaeza, 'enclosed garden') that the LXX uses for Eden and that Second Temple literature applies to the heavenly dwelling of the righteous dead — compare 2 Corinthians 12:4 (Paul caught up 'into paradise'), Revelation 2:7, and the locations described in 1 Enoch and 2 Enoch. So Luke 23:43 places Jesus (and the criminal) in the garden-abode of the righteous.

The harmonizing tradition is venerable and internally coherent: Augustine and Aquinas worked out itineraries in which the souls of the dead inhabited distinct compartments (the 'limbo of the fathers,' the place of the righteous, the prison of the damned), so that Christ between death and resurrection could visit more than one locale — preaching liberation to some, proclaiming judgment to others. On that scheme Luke's paradeisos and 1 Peter's phylake are simply two stops on one post-mortem journey, and there is no contradiction. The weakness is that this synthesis is a later theological construction; neither Luke nor 1 Peter shows any awareness of the other's geography or of a multi-stage itinerary. The texts are independent traditions, each using a different apocalyptic motif for a different purpose: Luke deploys paradise to dramatize individual salvation through the cross, while 1 Peter deploys the descent-to-the-Watchers to assert the cosmic scope of Christ's victory over hostile powers.

Steel-manned, the harmonization is logically possible and was historically influential, which is why this is rated partially rather than not harmonized. But it succeeds only by superimposing a synthetic later schema on two authors who never coordinated their claims; and it cannot rehabilitate the SAB's 'hell,' since the Petrine destination is the phylake of the Watchers, not a place of human damnation. Verdict: the surface 'heaven vs. hell' contradiction is overstated/misframed; what remains is two independent apocalyptic traditions, reconcilable only via a later harmonizing scheme.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The two destinations are described in different technical vocabularies — Luke's paradeisos (the heavenly garden of the righteous dead) and 1 Peter's phylake (the prison of the disobedient spirits/Watchers) — which are not the same place and not the medieval 'hell.' A complex post-mortem itinerary (developed by Augustine and Aquinas) can hold both, though neither text develops such a scheme; they are two independent traditions, not a flat contradiction.

entries.question: Who makes people blind?
entries.summary: Exodus 4:11 has Yahweh personally claim authorship over blindness, deafness, and muteness — they are direct acts of God. Mark 9:17-25, by contrast, treats deafness and muteness as the work of a foul spirit that Jesus exorcises, and John 9:1-3 treats congenital blindness as a setup for a divine demonstration rather than a curse to be undone. The Hebrew Bible's strict monotheistic etiology of disability collides with the Synoptic demonology that develops in the Second Temple period.
entries.commentary:
Here's the thing — Exodus 4:11 is unambiguous. Yahweh is asserting sole agency over sensory disability as part of his self-justification to Moses. The verb is qal active: "Who makes (sam) a person mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, Yahweh?" There's no demonic intermediary in the picture. The text reflects what John Collins calls the radically monistic theology of the priestly and Deuteronomistic traditions — Yahweh is the sole causal agent for both prosperity and calamity (cf. Isaiah 45:7, Amos 3:6).

By the time you get to Mark, the entire causal universe has been repopulated. Mark 9:25 explicitly names the spirit "deaf and dumb" (to alalon kai kophon pneuma) and commands it to leave — the disability is the spirit. This is straight Second Temple demonology, the kind you find in 1 Enoch, Jubilees, and the Qumran exorcism fragments. The apologist move here is to say these are separate cases — God causes some disabilities, demons cause others, and there's no contradiction. The apologist playbook, page one. The problem is that Exodus 4:11 is framed as a universal etiological claim, not a case-by-case attribution. Yahweh isn't saying "I make some blind people" — he's making a sweeping claim of authorship to ground Moses' commission.

The John 9:1-3 passage adds a third theological layer: blindness as a setup for divine theater. Raymond Brown notes that John pointedly rejects both Deuteronomic retributive justice (this man didn't sin, his parents didn't sin) and the Synoptic demonological frame — instead, blindness exists "so that the works of God might be revealed in him." That's a third etiology, not a harmonization. Three different theological universes, three different causal agents.

Exodus 4:11 is unambiguous. Yahweh, overriding Moses' protest about his speech, asserts sole agency over sensory capacity and incapacity: "Who makes (sam, qal active participle of sim) a person mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, Yahweh?" There is no intermediary in the picture — no Satan, no demon, no foul spirit. The statement is framed as a universal etiological claim grounding Moses' commission: because Yahweh controls speech and the senses, he can equip Moses' mouth. This fits what John Collins describes as the strongly monistic theology running through much of the Hebrew Bible, in which Yahweh is the single causal source of both weal and woe. The same theology speaks in Isaiah 45:7 ("I form light and create darkness, I make weal and create woe; I, Yahweh, do all these things") and Amos 3:6 ("Does disaster befall a city, unless Yahweh has done it?"). In this frame disability is not the work of a rival power; it is within Yahweh's direct authorship.

By the time of Mark the causal universe has been repopulated. Mark 9:25 names the spirit directly — to alalon kai kōphon pneuma, "the mute and deaf spirit" — and Jesus commands it to come out and enter the boy no more. The disability is not merely afflicted by the spirit; in Mark's idiom the spirit is characterized by, and produces, the muteness and deafness, and removing the spirit removes the condition. This is characteristic Second Temple demonology, a development largely absent from the older strata of the Hebrew Bible and well attested in the literature of the intertestamental period: the Watcher myth and origin of evil spirits in 1 Enoch 15-16, the demonology of Jubilees, and the exorcistic and apotropaic texts from Qumran (e.g., 4Q560, 11Q11). Archie Wright traces how Genesis 6:1-4 was reread to generate a population of malevolent spirits responsible for human affliction — a conceptual shift that gives the Synoptic exorcism narratives their causal backdrop. Joel Marcus, in the Anchor Yale Mark, situates the chapter 9 episode squarely within this framework.

The harmonizing response is to treat these as different cases: God authors some conditions, demons cause others, and Exodus 4:11 and Mark 9 simply describe distinct instances with no logical conflict. Stated fairly, this is not unreasonable on its own — the New Testament does not deny divine sovereignty, and one could hold that God permits or even ordains what demons execute (the Joban model of mediated affliction). The difficulty is that Exodus 4:11 is not phrased as a case-by-case attribution. It is a sweeping rhetorical claim of authorship — "Is it not I, Yahweh?" — deployed precisely to assert that no other agent stands behind speech or the senses. To then introduce an independent demonic etiology for the same class of conditions is to qualify a claim the Exodus text frames as unqualified. The two texts reflect different theological worlds, not two halves of one coherent doctrine of disability.

John 9:1-3 supplies a third etiology that resists assimilation to either of the first two. The disciples assume a Deuteronomic retributive model — someone sinned, the man or his parents — and Jesus rejects it outright: "Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but that the works of God might be revealed in him." That is neither the direct-divine-authorship claim of Exodus (the man's blindness is not presented as Yahweh's punitive or creative act) nor the demonological frame of Mark (no spirit is named); it is a teleological reframing in which a congenital condition exists to become the occasion of a revelatory sign. Raymond Brown notes that John here explicitly sets aside the retributive theology of suffering. Three texts, three different accounts of why a person cannot see or hear: sovereign divine making, demonic affliction, and providential staging of a sign.

Verdict: genuine theological development across the corpus, not a single coherent doctrine; the case-by-case harmonization founders on the universal phrasing of Exodus 4:11.

entries.question: Who raised Jesus from the dead?
entries.books_in_tension: John, Acts, Romans, Galatians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians
entries.summary: John 2:19-21 has Jesus declaring he will raise his own body in three days. Acts 2:24, 2:32, 4:10, 13:30, Galatians 1:1, Colossians 2:12, and 1 Thessalonians 1:10 all attribute the resurrection to God the Father, who raised Jesus. Romans 8:11 attributes it to the Holy Spirit. Three different agents across the New Testament for the same act, with the bulk of attestation going to the Father.
entries.commentary:
The orthodox harmonization is straightforward Trinitarian theology: all three persons act inseparably, and the resurrection is the work of the one God in three persons. That's a perfectly fine confessional answer, and it works on the dogmatic level. The historical-critical question is different — namely, what did the earliest Christians actually think happened, and did they think the same thing?

When you sort the verses chronologically you see something interesting. The earliest stratum — Paul's undisputed letters and the speeches in Acts (which preserve early creedal material) — overwhelmingly attribute the resurrection to God the Father acting on Jesus. *Ho theos auton ēgeiren ek nekrōn* ("God raised him from the dead") is one of the most common formulas in the New Testament. Jesus is the patient, God is the agent. This fits the early christological pattern that Bart Ehrman calls "exaltation Christology" — Jesus is a man whom God vindicated and exalted by raising him.

The John 2:19-21 saying — Jesus actively raising himself — is a Johannine theological development that aligns with John's high Christology of the pre-existent Logos. Even there, the narrator has to clarify that Jesus "spoke of the temple of his body," because the saying in its original form (cf. Mark 14:58, where the temple-destruction saying is preserved without the self-raising element) didn't necessarily imply self-resurrection. Romans 8:11 is the Spirit-resurrection tradition, which is rarer and appears to be a Pauline pneumatological emphasis rather than a developed doctrine.

The parsimonious read is developmental: the earliest formula is "God raised Jesus," the Pauline Spirit-formula is a side variant, and the Johannine self-raising formula is the latest theological refinement, made possible only after the Logos Christology was in place. You can call that a Trinitarian harmony retroactively, or you can call it three stages of Christological development. The data is the same; the interpretive frame is what changes.

commentary_out.commentary:
The orthodox harmonization is straightforward Trinitarian theology: under the principle that the external works of the Trinity are undivided (opera trinitatis ad extra indivisa sunt), all three persons act inseparably, so the resurrection is the single work of the one God subsisting in three persons. On the dogmatic level this resolves the tension cleanly, and it is the standard reading from the patristic period through the Reformers. The historical-critical question is different — namely, what the earliest Christians actually thought happened, and whether the New Testament writers were each saying the same thing.

The grammatical data is the place to begin. The dominant formula across the New Testament is built on the verb *egeirō*, "to raise," almost always in the form *ho theos ēgeiren auton ek nekrōn* ("God raised him from the dead") — Acts 2:24, 2:32, 4:10, 13:30, plus Gal 1:1, Col 2:12, 1 Thess 1:10, Rom 4:24, 10:9, 1 Cor 6:14, 15:15. Here Jesus is the grammatical object (the patient) and God the Father is the subject (the agent). A parallel set of texts uses the so-called "divine passive" — *ēgerthē*, "he was raised" (e.g., 1 Cor 15:4, Rom 6:4) — where the unstated agent is understood to be God. In neither construction does Jesus act on himself. This fits the early Christological pattern Bart Ehrman terms "exaltation Christology": Jesus is the one whom God vindicated, raised, and exalted to lordship (cf. the pre-Pauline formula embedded in Rom 1:3-4 and Phil 2:9, where God is the one who "highly exalted" him).

The John 2:19-21 saying breaks this pattern. There Jesus speaks in the active/future — "in three days I will raise it up" (*en trisin hēmerais egerō auton*) — making himself the agent of his own resurrection. This is distinctively Johannine and coheres with the Fourth Gospel's high Logos Christology and the explicit claim of John 10:18, "I have authority to lay [my life] down, and I have authority to take it up again." Tellingly, the Johannine narrator must gloss the saying: "But he was speaking of the temple of his body" (2:21). This redactional clarification is necessary precisely because the saying's traditional form did not carry a self-resurrection meaning. The Synoptic parallels preserve a temple-destruction saying placed on the lips of false witnesses (Mark 14:58; Matt 26:61) and the mocking taunt at the cross (Mark 15:29), all without any self-raising element — strong evidence that the original logion concerned the temple and was secondarily Christianized in John toward bodily resurrection.

Romans 8:11 supplies a third agent: "the Spirit of him who raised Jesus." Read closely the verse still makes God the one "who raised Jesus," but assigns the Spirit the role of agent in raising believers' mortal bodies, and the syntax allows the Spirit a role in Christ's resurrection as well. This pneumatological emphasis is rarer and looks like a Pauline development rather than a fixed formula.

The parsimonious reading is developmental. The earliest and most heavily attested formula is "God raised Jesus," rooted in the resurrection's function as divine vindication. The Pauline Spirit-language is a side variant tied to Paul's anthropology of the indwelling Spirit. The Johannine self-raising formula is the latest refinement, possible only once the pre-existent-Logos Christology was in place — which is why it surfaces in the Gospel most distant from the Synoptic tradition and requires an editorial gloss to land. One may retroject a Trinitarian harmony onto this data, and confessionally it holds; but the same evidence reads equally as three stages of Christological development. The data is constant; the interpretive frame is what changes. Verdict: harmonizable at the dogmatic level, but the underlying datum is genuine Christological development across strata.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: On the dogmatic level the inseparable-operations principle (opera trinitatis ad extra indivisa sunt) coherently assigns one act to three persons; the residual tension is historical-developmental, not logical, since the three agent-formulas represent successive Christological strata rather than a single coordinated claim.

entries.question: Is it OK to eat meat sacrificed to other gods?
entries.summary: 1 Corinthians 8:4-8 has Paul argue that since an idol is nothing, food sacrificed to it is theologically neutral — eating it neither commends nor condemns you to God. Acts 15:28-29 has the Jerusalem Council decree, as one of a handful of "necessary things" laid on Gentile believers by the Holy Ghost, that they must abstain from meat offered to idols. One text treats idol-meat as a matter of indifference governed only by love for a weaker brother; the other makes abstaining a binding apostolic requirement. They give incompatible answers to the same question.
entries.commentary:
A note on the correction first: this entry came in mis-titled as "Is circumcision required?", but the cited verses and the source page (SAB's /contra/meat.html, "Is it OK to eat meat sacrificed to other gods?") are about food offered to idols, not circumcision — a scraper join error. The verses themselves were correct, so the title has been re-aligned to the food-sacrificed-to-idols question the verses actually support, rather than swapping in the circumcision proof-texts. Everything below describes that real Pauline-vs-Lukan seam.

1 Corinthians 8:4-8: Paul argues that since idols are nothing, meat sacrificed to them is theologically neutral; eating it neither commends nor condemns. The only constraint is not to scandalize a weaker brother whose conscience is troubled. Acts 15:28-29: the Jerusalem Council under James decrees that Gentile believers must abstain from meat sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality. These are presented as binding (*epanankes* — "necessary").

Paul's stance in 1 Corinthians 8-10 (cf. Romans 14) treats the idol-meat question as a matter of Christian liberty conditioned only by love for the weaker member. The Jerusalem Council treats it as a categorical prohibition. F. F. Bruce and the conservative tradition try to reconcile these by reading the Acts 15 decree as a temporary local accommodation for Antioch and Asia Minor, not a universal mandate — and noting that Paul might have respected the decree in those areas while teaching liberty elsewhere. But Paul never references the Jerusalem decree in his letters, including in 1 Corinthians, where it would have settled the dispute. Paul's silence on the Apostolic Decree (Acts 15) is one of the most consistent indicators that either Luke composed the decree to harmonize the early church or Paul didn't consider himself bound by it. The critical consensus (Lüdemann, Dunn) is that Luke's Acts 15 is a theological reconstruction; the historical Paul taught liberty on this question without conditions.

The SAB entry, once you correct the question title, is pointing at a real seam between Pauline and Lukan accounts of early church teaching.

commentary_out.commentary:
A note on the correction first: this entry arrived mis-titled as "Is circumcision required?", but the cited verses and the source page (the Skeptic's Annotated Bible page on meat sacrificed to idols) concern food offered to idols, not circumcision — a scraper join error. The verses themselves were correct, so the title has been re-aligned to the question the verses actually support rather than swapping in the circumcision proof-texts. What follows describes that genuine Pauline-versus-Lukan seam.

In 1 Corinthians 8:4-8 Paul argues that "an idol is nothing in the world" (*ouden eidōlon en kosmō*) and that, in consequence, meat sacrificed to it — *eidōlothyton* — is theologically neutral: "food will not commend us to God; we are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do." The only operative constraint is pastoral: do not wound the conscience of the "weak" brother for whom the association with idolatry is still real (8:9-13), an argument Paul extends in 1 Cor 10:23-33 and parallels in Romans 14. The question is thus, for Paul, a matter of Christian liberty governed by love, not by law.

Acts 15:28-29 has the Jerusalem Council, under James, decree that Gentile believers must "abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality." Crucially, these are framed as binding — *epanankes*, "necessary things" — and authorized by the Holy Spirit ("it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"). On idol-meat specifically, Acts states a categorical prohibition where Paul states liberty.

The traditional harmonization (F. F. Bruce, Bruce Metzger on the textual side) reads the Decree as a localized, ad hoc accommodation for the mixed congregations of Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia — note the address in Acts 15:23 — aimed at preserving table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers, not as a universal and permanent code. On this reading Paul could honor the Decree's spirit in those regions while teaching liberty on the underlying theology elsewhere. This is genuinely plausible as far as it goes, and the categories of "things strangled" and "blood" point toward Jewish dietary scruples about table fellowship rather than abstract doctrine. The textual history reinforces the fluidity: the Western text (Codex Bezae and allies) drops "things strangled" and adds a negative form of the Golden Rule, transforming the Decree from a food code into a moral one — evidence that even early scribes were uncertain what the prohibitions were for.

The harmonization founders on Paul's silence. The Decree, if Paul knew of it and considered himself bound, would have settled the Corinthian dispute in a sentence — yet across the extended treatment of 1 Cor 8-10 Paul never cites it, never alludes to a Jerusalem ruling, and grounds his answer entirely in his own theology of the one God and the weak conscience. The same silence holds in Galatians 2, where Paul recounts the Jerusalem meeting and reports only that the pillars added nothing to him (Gal 2:6) — the opposite of an apostolic decree imposing four requirements. The critical assessment of Gerd Lüdemann is that Luke composed the Decree as a retrojected ecclesial compromise; James D. G. Dunn, more moderately, treats it as a historical accord whose terms Paul either did not accept as binding or understood differently than Luke presents. Either way, the historical Paul taught liberty on idol-meat without the categorical conditions Acts 15 attaches. Verdict: partially harmonizable as a local accommodation, but Paul's structural silence leaves a real Pauline-vs-Lukan tension.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The Decree can be read as a localized, ad hoc concord for the mixed Jewish-Gentile congregations of Syria and Cilicia (Acts 15:23) addressing table fellowship, while Paul teaches liberty on the abstract theological question elsewhere; the residual problem is Paul's total silence about the Decree where it would have settled his own disputes, which the harmonization cannot explain.

entries.question: Can women be church leaders?
entries.summary: Acts 18:26 has Priscilla (with her husband Aquila) instructing Apollos in "the way of God" — a clear example of a woman exercising teaching authority in the early church. 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 commands that women keep silent in the churches and not speak; 1 Timothy 2:11-12 prohibits women from teaching or having authority over a man. Pauline-attributed texts both permit and prohibit female leadership in the same canon.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the contradictions where the critical-scholarly explanation is overwhelming and the apologetic explanation is fragile. 1 Timothy is not from Paul — the Pastoral Epistles (1-2 Timothy, Titus) are pseudepigraphic in the mainstream critical consensus, going back through Bauckham, Brown, and Ehrman. The vocabulary, the church-order concerns (overseers, deacons, widow lists), the polemic against "myths and endless genealogies," and the institutional setting all point to a late first or early second century author writing in Paul's name. So when 1 Timothy 2:11-12 prohibits women teaching, it's not Paul making that prohibition — it's a later Pauline-school author trying to constrain a Pauline tradition that had been more egalitarian.

1 Corinthians 14:34-35 is a different problem. Many critical scholars (Fee, Conzelmann, Ehrman) argue these verses are an interpolation. They interrupt the flow of Paul's argument about prophecy, they appear in different positions in some manuscripts (after 14:40 in the Western text tradition), and they directly contradict 1 Corinthians 11:5, where Paul assumes women are prophesying and praying in the assembly — he just wants them to do it with their heads covered. The textual evidence is suggestive enough that NA28 and several major critical commentaries treat 14:34-35 as possibly secondary.

Meanwhile, the egalitarian side of the canon is robust. Romans 16 names Phoebe as a deacon (*diakonos*) and Junia as outstanding among the apostles. Priscilla is consistently named before her husband Aquila — unusual in the ancient world and suggesting her prominence. Galatians 3:28 — neither male nor female in Christ — is a baptismal formula Paul cites approvingly. The apologist (Köstenberger, Schreiner) tries to reconcile by limiting the egalitarian texts to specific contexts and giving the restrictive texts universal force. The critical reading reverses that: the egalitarian practice is original, and the restrictive texts are either interpolations or pseudepigraphic walk-backs. Take your pick on which Paul to follow — but the historical Paul looks a lot more like the one who worked with Priscilla and Junia than the one who silences women in 1 Timothy.

				          unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience as
				          also saith the law. And if they will learn any thing, let them ask

commentary_out.commentary:
The canon speaks with at least two voices on women's leadership, and the critical and complementarian camps resolve the dissonance in opposite directions. The data points are clear. Acts 18:26 has Priscilla, named with Aquila, *akribesteron autō exethento tēn hodon tou theou* — they "explained the way of God more accurately" to the learned Apollos, an unambiguous instance of a woman exercising doctrinal instruction. Romans 16 reinforces the egalitarian picture: Phoebe is a *diakonos* and *prostatis* of the church at Cenchreae (16:1-2), and Junia is *episēmoi en tois apostolois* — "outstanding among the apostles" (16:7), a reading Epp and the patristic witnesses (Chrysostom calls her an apostle) defend against the later masculinizing "Junias." Against this stand 1 Corinthians 14:34-35, commanding women to keep silent (*sigatōsan*) in the assemblies, and 1 Timothy 2:11-12, forbidding a woman *didaskein* or *authentein andros* — to teach or exercise authority over a man.

The critical resolution operates on two fronts. First, the Pastoral Epistles are widely judged pseudepigraphic. Since Holtzmann's nineteenth-century work and through Brown, Bauckham, and Ehrman, the case rests on a vocabulary statistically divergent from the undisputed Paulines, a developed church order (overseers, deacons, enrolled-widow lists), a polemic against "myths and endless genealogies" suiting a second-century setting, and a domesticated ethic remote from the apocalyptic urgency of 1 Corinthians 7. If 1 Timothy is a Pauline-school product of c. 100-130 CE, then 2:11-12 is not Paul restricting women but a later author constraining a tradition that had been more open — and even grounding the restriction in a reading of Genesis (Eve deceived first) that Paul nowhere else deploys.

Second, 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 carries its own text-critical cloud. The verses float: in the Western tradition (Codex Claromontanus, Codex Fuldensis marginalia, and the minuscules of family D) they appear after 14:40 rather than after 14:33. Fee and Conzelmann argue that this floating, combined with the direct collision with 1 Corinthians 11:5 — where Paul regulates rather than forbids women praying and prophesying in the assembly — marks 14:34-35 as a post-Pauline interpolation, possibly imported from the same milieu that produced 1 Timothy 2. Fitzmyer is more cautious, retaining the verses while conceding the gravity of the displacement evidence. Either way, the silence command sits awkwardly four chapters after Paul presupposes women speaking.

The complementarian harmonization, represented by Schreiner and Köstenberger, is not a strawman and deserves its strongest form: they argue the texts address distinct functions and so do not contradict. Priscilla's instruction of Apollos was private (in their home, with her husband), not authoritative public teaching over the gathered church; Phoebe's *diakonos* role was service, not governance; and the prohibitions in 1 Corinthians 14 and 1 Timothy 2 target the authoritative teaching office and the public evaluation of prophecy. On this reading the canon is consistent: women minister broadly but do not hold the specific office of authoritative teacher-elder. The reading is internally coherent and takes the texts as a unified Pauline whole.

It founders on two assumptions the critical reading rejects. It must treat all the texts as genuinely Pauline and roughly contemporaneous, which the pseudepigraphy of the Pastorals undercuts; and it must read the restrictive texts as the interpretive key that domesticates the permissive ones, when the historical and text-critical evidence points the other way — toward an earlier egalitarian practice (Galatians 3:28, Junia, Phoebe, Priscilla) that was progressively narrowed, as MacDonald traces, by interpolation and pseudepigraphic walk-back. The disagreement is therefore not merely exegetical but turns on authorship, dating, and textual integrity, which is why the status here is best labeled disputed rather than cleanly harmonized or not. Verdict: a genuine canonical tension whose resolution depends entirely on contested judgments about Pauline authorship — the historical Paul looks far more like the colleague of Priscilla and Junia than the silencer of 1 Timothy.
commentary_out.change_summary: Deepened the pseudepigraphy case for the Pastorals, the interpolation evidence for 1 Cor 14:34-35 (manuscript displacement, vellum marginalia), the Romans 16/Junia data, and the complementarian counter-case; roughly doubled length.
