The transposition is found in the Western witnesses D F G (and it. mss), and Codex Fuldensis (Vulgate) has Victor of Capua's marginal note bearing on the passage. Calling these 'the minuscules of family D' is imprecise — D F G are majuscule/uncial Western witnesses, not minuscules of a 'family D.' entries.question: Should believers discuss their faith with non-believers?
entries.summary: 1 Peter 3:15 commands believers to be ready always to give an answer to anyone who asks for a reason for the hope in them. Colossians 4:5-6 echoes this with speech seasoned with salt toward outsiders. But 2 John 1:10 forbids even receiving anyone who brings a different doctrine into your house, and 1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 2:16 command shunning profane and vain babblings. Engage outsiders, or shun them — the New Testament does both.
entries.commentary: The texts are talking past each other because they assume different audiences. 1 Peter 3:15 envisions a Christian minority pressed by hostile outsiders demanding to know why these people are different — the *apologia* (defense) is reactive and requires intelligible engagement. Colossians 4:5-6 likewise prescribes outward-facing speech. The Johannine and Pastoral texts envision a different scenario: itinerant teachers carrying heterodox versions of the gospel into believing households, where the rule becomes shun-and-don't-engage. 2 John 1:10's prohibition is specifically about the docetist Christology that the Johannine letters fight throughout (1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 7). The Pastorals' "profane babblings" (*bebēlous kenophōnias*) refers to proto-Gnostic speculation. Apologetic harmonization, articulated by Karen Jobes and George Knight, says these texts address different scenarios: outsiders genuinely seeking get an apologia; insider teachers spreading false doctrine get shunned. That distinction is real and largely correct as exegesis. The contradiction is partially overstated by SAB's framing, but it isn't fully resolved either. The Pastoral epistles deploy *kenophōnias* and the Johannine letters deploy heretic-shunning language in ways that have historically been weaponized against any external engagement, and the texts themselves don't sharply mark the in-group/out-group distinction the harmonization requires. The contradiction is functionally less about whether to discuss faith with non-believers and more about how internally consistent the NT is on doctrinal engagement with dissenters. A coherency note is warranted.

answers.answer_explanation:
Be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope 
				        that is in you with meekness and fear. 1 Peter 3:15
				        
				        Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time. Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt,
				 that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man. Colossians 4:5-6

If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, 
				        neither bid him God speed. 2 John 1:10
				        
				        O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science 
				        falsely so called: Which some professing have erred concerning the faith. 1 Timothy 6:20-21
				        
				        
But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. 
				        2 Timothy 2:16

commentary_out.commentary:
These texts conflict only if read as context-free rules about a single activity; on inspection they address different situations and different audiences. 1 Peter 3:15 envisions a Christian minority under social pressure: believers are to be ready to make a *apologia* (a reasoned defense) "to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you," and explicitly "with gentleness and reverence." The setting is reactive — outsiders, sometimes hostile, demanding an account of why these people live differently (cf. 3:14-16, the surrounding language of suffering and slander). Colossians 4:5-6 is the positive counterpart: "walk in wisdom toward outsiders (*pros tous exō*)... let your speech be always gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer each person." Both texts are outward-facing and assume intelligible engagement with non-believers.

The prohibitions come from a different scenario. 2 John 1:10 — "if anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house or give him any greeting" — is not about evangelistic dialogue with the unconverted at all. Its target is itinerant teachers carrying a deviant Christology into believing households; the surrounding letters define the error precisely as the denial that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 7), i.e., an early docetic or proto-Gnostic teaching. The "house" in view is very likely the house-church, and "receiving" connotes offering hospitality and a platform. Similarly, the Pastoral injunctions to avoid "profane chatter" (*bebēlous kenophōnias*, 1 Tim 6:20) and the "falsely-named knowledge" (*pseudōnymou gnōseōs*) and to "shun profane and empty babblings" (2 Tim 2:16) target speculative teaching circulating within or pressing upon the congregation — language that scholars from I. Howard Marshall to Raymond Collins read against an emergent proto-Gnostic milieu.

The apologetic harmonization, voiced by Karen Jobes and George Knight, draws exactly this distinction: genuine outsiders who inquire receive a courteous *apologia*; insiders or itinerants peddling false doctrine receive disengagement. This is sound exegesis as far as it goes, and the texts do operate in different registers — public witness versus protection of community boundaries. So the contradiction as the skeptic frames it — "engage outsiders or shun them" — is partly a category error, since the shunning texts are aimed at heterodox teachers, not at non-believers being witnessed to.

That said, the resolution is not airtight. The texts themselves do not crisply mark the in-group/out-group line the harmonization needs. 2 John's "if anyone comes" is unqualified, and the docetists in question presumably claimed to be Christians, so the boundary between "false insider" and "outsider with a different view" is precisely what is contested. The Pastorals' commands to "avoid" and "shun" speculative talk have, throughout Christian history, been read as warrants against any external doctrinal engagement, and Brown, Lieu, and Collins note that the Johannine and Pastoral communities were drawing sharp sectarian boundaries that sit uneasily beside 1 Peter's irenic, dialogical posture. The deeper issue is therefore not whether to speak with non-believers — on that the texts are reconcilable — but how consistent the New Testament is on engaging dissent, where a genuinely different communal ethos shows through: 1 Peter and Colossians encourage open, gracious engagement, while the Johannine and Pastoral letters counsel separation from doctrinal opponents. Verdict: overstated as a flat contradiction (the texts address different audiences), but a real residual tension remains between the dialogical and the boundary-drawing strands of the New Testament.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The texts address different audiences and situations: 1 Peter and Colossians prescribe a gracious apologia to inquiring outsiders, whereas 2 John and the Pastorals prescribe shunning heterodox teachers (docetists; proto-Gnostic speculation) carrying false doctrine into the community. This dissolves the surface 'engage vs. shun non-believers' framing, but a real residual tension remains between the dialogical and boundary-drawing ethos of these communities.

entries.question: Was Rahab saved by faith or works?
entries.summary: Hebrews 11:31 says Rahab the harlot did not perish with the disobedient because of her faith when she received the spies. James 2:25 says Rahab was justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way. Same Old Testament figure, same single act (hiding the Israelite spies in Joshua 2), two contradictory verdicts on what saved her.
entries.commentary: This is the same Pauline-vs-Jacobean tension that appears around Abraham (see id 542), now applied to Rahab. Hebrews places Rahab in its great roll-call of faith heroes — *pistei Raab hē pornē* — and credits her preservation to faith. James 2:25 zeroes in on the same episode and credits her justification to works (*ex ergōn*). Both texts cite the same act: hospitable concealment of the spies. The harmonization, articulated by Douglas Moo and Peter Davids, runs through the faith-as-demonstrated-by-works framework: Rahab's reception of the spies was the visible expression of her underlying faith, so both authors are describing the same reality from different angles. That harmonization works at the systematic-theology level but it requires importing later categories — the medieval *fides quae* / *fides qua* distinction, or Reformation faith-and-works syntheses — that neither author articulates. Critical scholarship from Luke Timothy Johnson, Dale Allison, and Harold Attridge treats Hebrews 11 as drawing on Jewish-Hellenistic exemplar traditions (Sirach 44, 4 Maccabees) where faith and faithful action are intertwined, while James 2 is explicitly polemicizing against a faith-alone reading — likely a misreading of Paul. The contradiction reflects two early Christian streams disagreeing about how Rahab's salvation works, with both texts authorized as canonical scripture. Whatever harmonization is possible at the doctrinal level, the canonical text places these two verdicts in unresolved juxtaposition. Rahab is the rare figure both authors reach for, and that's exactly why the disagreement is sharpest.

answers.answer_explanation:
By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that
			          believed not, when she had received the spies with peace. 
			          Hebrews 11:31

Was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she
			          had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way? 
			          James 2:25

commentary_out.commentary:
Rahab is the sharpest test case for the faith-versus-works tension precisely because both authors reach for the same single episode — the concealment of the Israelite spies in Joshua 2 — and render opposite verdicts on what secured her deliverance. Hebrews 11:31 enrolls her in its catalogue of faith: *pistei Raab hē pornē ou synapōleto tois apeithēsasin* — "by faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, having received the spies in peace." The instrumental dative *pistei* ("by faith") is the anaphoric refrain that governs the entire chapter, attributing her survival to faith. James 2:25 invokes the identical event with the opposite causal term: *homoiōs de kai Raab hē pornē ouk ex ergōn edikaiōthē, hypodexamenē tous angelous kai hetera hodō ekbalousa?* — "was not Rahab the prostitute likewise justified *by works* (*ex ergōn*) when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by another road?" The verb *edikaiōthē* ("was justified") is forensic, and *ex ergōn* is exactly the prepositional phrase Paul negates in Romans 3:28 and Galatians 2:16. James is not using neutral vocabulary; he is using the Pauline slogan and reversing its polarity.

That is the crux. James 2 is not merely emphasizing good behavior in general; it is explicitly polemicizing against a "faith alone" position: "a person is justified by works and not by faith alone" (2:24, *ouk ek pisteōs monon*), and "faith without works is dead" (2:26). Whether James targets Paul directly or a misapplication of Pauline teaching is debated — Dale Allison and Richard Bauckham favor a corrective aimed at a distorted Paulinism circulating in James's milieu — but in either case James deliberately deploys the same triad (faith, works, justification) and the same scriptural exemplars (Abraham in 2:21-23, Rahab in 2:25) to reach the opposite conclusion from the one those exemplars carry in the Pauline and the Hebrews traditions.

The standard harmonization, articulated by Douglas Moo and Peter Davids, runs through the "faith demonstrated by works" synthesis: Rahab's reception of the spies was the outward enactment of an inward faith (she confesses YHWH's supremacy in Joshua 2:9-11), so Hebrews names the root and James names the fruit, and both describe one reality. At the level of systematic theology this is coherent and has a long pedigree. Its weakness is historical and exegetical: it imports a reconciling framework — the scholastic distinction between the faith by which one believes and the works that evidence it, or the Reformation synthesis of justification and sanctification — that neither author states. Luke Timothy Johnson, Harold Attridge, and Craig Koester locate Hebrews 11 within Hellenistic-Jewish exemplar catalogues (Sirach 44-50; 4 Maccabees 16:20-23; Wisdom 10) in which "faith" and "faithful deeds" are fused and not analytically separated, while James belongs to a distinct, deliberately anti-"faith-alone" trajectory. The two writers are not collaborating on a single doctrine viewed from two angles; they are participants in an intra-Christian dispute about how salvation is appropriated, and the canon preserves both unreconciled.

Thus while the propositions can be synthesized at the level of later dogmatics, the texts themselves stand in unresolved juxtaposition: Hebrews says Rahab was preserved *by faith*; James says she was justified *by works and not by faith alone*; and James says so using the precise vocabulary Hebrews and Paul would have answered differently. Verdict: genuine theological contradiction at the level of the texts' own formulations, harmonizable only by importing a later synthetic framework neither author shares.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: On the 'faith demonstrated by works' synthesis, Hebrews names the root (faith) and James names its visible fruit (the works that evidence it), both describing Rahab's single act in Joshua 2. The synthesis is coherent as systematic theology but requires importing a faith/works framework neither author articulates; at the level of their own wording (pistei vs. ex ergōn… ouk ek pisteōs monon) the verdicts stand in unresolved juxtaposition.

entries.question: Can visual stimuli during conception affect the appearance of offspring?
entries.summary: Genesis 30:39 has Jacob's flocks conceiving in front of peeled striped rods and then producing striped and spotted lambs. The text is making a biological claim — that what an animal looks at while mating influences the genetics of its offspring. This is maternal impression theory, and it is not how heredity works. Coat patterns come from alleles, not from what mom was staring at.
entries.commentary: The standard apologetic dodge here is to say God supernaturally produced the speckled offspring and Jacob's rods were just incidental — Walton in the IVP Bible Background Commentary leans this way. But that reading is a retrofit. The text gives no indication that the rods are decorative. Genesis 30:37-39 spells out a deliberate procedure: Jacob peels the rods, sets them in the watering troughs where the strongest animals come to drink and mate, and the flocks "conceived before the rods" and produced spotted offspring. The causal logic of the passage is that the visual exposure produced the phenotype. This is precisely the ancient Near Eastern folk belief in maternal impression — the idea that what a pregnant animal or woman saw could imprint on the fetus. It shows up in Pliny the Elder, in Soranus, in medieval bestiaries. Hermann Gunkel in his Genesis commentary identifies the rods explicitly as sympathetic magic, and Claus Westermann in the Continental Commentary treats it the same way. Even John Walton, who wants to preserve the historicity, admits this is operating on "ancient principles of animal husbandry" that are not scientifically valid. So the apologist has to choose: either the text means what it says and the biology is wrong, or the text is doing folklore and we shouldn't expect it to track modern genetics. Either way, the claim that visual stimuli at conception affects offspring is false, and the narrator of Genesis 30 presents it as if it works. That is of course a subjective reading of intent, but the syntax of verses 37-39 makes the causal chain hard to wave away.

answers.answer: The Bible claims striped rods caused striped offspring
answers.answer_explanation: And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted. (Genesis 30:39)

commentary_out.commentary:
Genesis 30:25-43 narrates Jacob's stratagem against Laban. After agreeing to take the speckled, spotted, and dark animals as his wages, Jacob takes fresh rods of poplar, almond, and plane, peels white streaks into them to expose the lighter wood, and sets the peeled rods in the watering troughs "before the flocks" at the time of mating (Gen 30:37-38). The text then states the outcome with deliberate causal force: "And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted" (Gen 30:39). The Hebrew syntax binds the conception to the visual exposure — the animals mate while looking at the streaked rods, and the offspring bear the corresponding markings. This is a textbook instance of what historians of biology call maternal impression: the folk belief, widespread across the ancient Mediterranean and Near East, that visual or emotional stimuli experienced at conception or during gestation imprint physically on the offspring. The belief is documented in Pliny the Elder's Natural History, in the gynecological writings of Soranus of Ephesus, and persisted into medieval bestiaries and early modern medicine. Genetically the claim is false: coat pattern in sheep and goats is determined by alleles inherited from both parents, not by what a ewe perceives while mating.

The strongest harmonization does not dispute the biology but relocates the causation. Drawing on Genesis 31:10-12 — where Jacob recounts a dream in which the angel of God tells him that the rams mounting the flock were striped, speckled, and grizzled, and that God had seen Laban's deceit — apologists such as the IVP Bible Background Commentary and Walton argue that the speckled offspring were a divine act, and that Jacob's rods were either incidental, an expression of his own folk belief that God then accommodated, or simply ineffective superstition that the narrator does not endorse. On this reading Genesis 31 functions as the theological key that retroactively explains Genesis 30: God, not the rods, produced the result.

This reading has genuine textual purchase, because Genesis 31:10-12 unquestionably attributes the increase to God, and a redactor combining the two notices may well have intended the dream to override the magic. But it does not erase the difficulty in Genesis 30 itself. Chapter 30 spells out a deliberate, repeated, and selectively applied procedure: Jacob uses the rods only when the stronger animals breed and withholds them for the feebler, so that the strong stock becomes his and the weak Laban's (Gen 30:41-42). That is not the language of incidental decoration; it is the language of a technique the narrator presents as working through sympathetic influence. Hermann Gunkel identified the rods as sympathetic magic, and Claus Westermann read the episode the same way, as folkloric etiology for Jacob's prosperity. Nahum Sarna and Gordon Wenham likewise treat the peeled-rod motif as reflecting ancient husbandry beliefs rather than genetics. The most plausible source-critical account is that two explanations of Jacob's wealth — one magical (ch. 30) and one theological (ch. 31) — stand side by side in the text, the latter perhaps a later interpretive overlay. The divine-attribution harmonization succeeds at the level of the final canonical form but only by conceding that the procedure described in chapter 30 reflects a biologically false belief that the narrator there presents as efficacious. Verdict: the underlying biological claim is folklore, not science; partially recoverable theologically via Gen 31 but not as natural history.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Genesis 31:10-12 attributes the speckled offspring to God rather than the rods, so at the canonical level the increase can be read as divine action and the rods as ineffective folk practice; this rescues the theology but concedes that Genesis 30:37-42 presents the visual-impression procedure as biologically effective, which it is not.

entries.question: How many apostles were in office between the resurrection and ascension?
entries.summary: Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:5 reports that the risen Jesus appeared "to Cephas, then to the twelve." But by the time of the resurrection, Judas Iscariot had already died (Matthew 27:3-5), and Matthew 28:16 explicitly calls the post-resurrection group "the eleven disciples." Acts 1:9 has Jesus ascending while the eleven look on, and Matthias is not selected until Acts 1:26. So between resurrection and ascension the apostolic college numbered eleven, not twelve.
entries.commentary: The apologetic move here is to say "the twelve" is a titular collective name for the apostolic group — like calling a sports team "the Bulls" even when one player is injured. Anthony Thiselton in the NIGTC 1 Corinthians commentary and Gordon Fee in the NICNT both adopt this reading: "the twelve" functions as a fixed designation for the apostolic body regardless of actual membership. That's a defensible reading and it's probably what Paul means. But it doesn't fully dissolve the tension — Paul is reporting a resurrection appearance, presumably with a specific historical referent, and at the moment of that appearance the group physically present numbered eleven men. The standard critical observation, made by Hans Conzelmann in the Hermeneia 1 Corinthians, is that Paul is quoting an early creedal formula (1 Corinthians 15:3-5) that pre-dates his letter. The formula's use of "the twelve" probably reflects pre-Pauline tradition that hadn't yet been harmonized with the Judas-betrayal narrative. There's an even deeper problem: the textual variants. Some witnesses read "the eleven" instead of "the twelve" in 1 Corinthians 15:5 — Bruce Metzger's *Textual Commentary* discusses this. The fact that scribes felt the need to correct the number to eleven shows that ancient readers also saw the conflict. So either Paul (or his pre-formed creed) is using "the twelve" as a fixed title that doesn't track actual headcount, or there's an unresolved tension between the Pauline tradition and the gospel narratives about Judas. The titular reading is defensible but it concedes that the number is not literal — which means the contradiction is real at the level of arithmetic and only dissolves at the level of conventional usage.

answers.answer_explanation: And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve: (1 Corinthians 15:5)

Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, (Matthew 27:3)

Then the eleven disciples went away into Galilee, into a mountain where Jesus had appointed them. (Matthew 28:16)

And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. (Acts 1:9)

commentary_out.commentary:
The tension is straightforward arithmetic. Paul's creed in 1 Corinthians 15:5 reports that the risen Jesus appeared "to Cephas, then to the twelve" (*tois dōdeka*). Yet the gospel narratives are unanimous that Judas Iscariot was already dead by the resurrection: Matthew 27:3-5 has him hang himself before the crucifixion, and Matthew 28:16 calls the post-resurrection group "the eleven disciples" (*hoi hendeka mathētai*). Luke-Acts agrees — Luke 24:33 has "the eleven," Acts 1:9 shows "the eleven" watching the ascension, and Matthias is not enrolled until Acts 1:26. Between resurrection and ascension the apostolic body physically numbered eleven.

The leading harmonization treats "the Twelve" as a fixed titular designation for the apostolic institution rather than a literal headcount — comparable to a team name that persists when a roster slot is vacant. Anthony Thiselton (NIGTC) and Gordon Fee (NICNT) both adopt this, and it is almost certainly what the formula intends: *hoi dōdeka* had become a near-technical term for the inner circle Jesus had constituted. John P. Meier's influential JBL study argues persuasively that "the Twelve" was an actual pre-Easter institution founded by Jesus himself, symbolizing the restoration of the twelve tribes of Israel — which is exactly why the title would survive a temporary vacancy and why Acts moves quickly to fill it (Acts 1:15-26). On this reading the number twelve is symbolic-institutional, not a census.

That resolution is reasonable but it does not fully erase the friction, for two reasons. First, the creed is reporting a specific historical resurrection appearance with a concrete referent; at the moment described, the men present numbered eleven, so the title outruns the fact. Second, and more tellingly, the manuscript tradition records that ancient readers felt the same pinch. Several witnesses read "the eleven" (*tois hendeka*) at 1 Corinthians 15:5 — the reading is noted in the apparatus and discussed by Metzger — a transparent scribal correction to bring the count into line with the gospels. The existence of the variant is evidence that the discrepancy was perceived from antiquity.

The source-critical layer deepens the picture. Hans Conzelmann (Hermeneia) and Gerd Lüdemann emphasize that 1 Corinthians 15:3-5 is a pre-Pauline creedal formula that Paul received and quotes; its language predates not only this letter but very likely the written gospel passion narratives. "The Twelve" in this primitive confession reflects an early Christian tradition that had not yet been coordinated with the developed Judas-betrayal story. The formula preserves an archaic naming convention; the gospels supply a narrative (Judas's death, the interregnum, Matthias's selection) that the formula never accommodated.

So the titular reading is correct and defensible — but it resolves the problem precisely by conceding that the number is not literal. The contradiction is genuine at the level of arithmetic and dissolves only at the level of conventional, institutional usage, with the additional likelihood that the creed simply antedates the Judas tradition it appears to ignore. Verdict: harmonizable as a fixed title, but the harmonization concedes the count is non-literal, and the variant tradition shows the tension was felt early.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: "The Twelve" functions as a fixed institutional/titular designation for the apostolic circle Jesus founded (symbolic of the twelve tribes), surviving the temporary vacancy left by Judas, rather than a literal census; this resolves the usage but concedes the number is non-literal, and the pre-Pauline creed likely predates the developed Judas narrative.

entries.question: Does God destroy man for his wickedness?
entries.summary: Genesis 6:5-7 has God resolving to destroy humanity precisely because "the wickedness of man was great" and "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually." After the flood, Genesis 8:21 has the same God promising never again to curse the ground or smite all living things for man's sake — and giving as his reason "for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth." The exact same reason that motivated the flood is now cited as a reason NOT to flood again.
entries.commentary: This is one of the cleaner contradictions in Genesis because the same Hebrew phrase — *yetser libbo ra* (the inclination of his heart is evil) — appears in both verses, and it functions as the explicit grounds for opposite divine decisions. In Genesis 6:5 the evil inclination triggers destruction; in Genesis 8:21 it triggers forbearance. Apologists like Kenneth Mathews in the NAC Genesis volume try to harmonize by saying that 8:21 reflects God's mercy responding to Noah's sacrifice — the post-flood promise is a new covenantal move that doesn't contradict the pre-flood judgment because circumstances have changed. That works narratively but it doesn't dissolve the contradiction in the divine reasoning. The text doesn't say "because of Noah's sacrifice I will hold back." It says "because man's heart is evil from his youth I will hold back" — using the evil inclination as the *reason for restraint*. This is one of the strongest pieces of source-critical evidence for the JEDP hypothesis. Critical scholars from Hermann Gunkel to Claus Westermann to Joel Baden have noted that Genesis 6 and Genesis 8 carry different sources within the flood narrative — Genesis 6:5-8 is widely assigned to J (the Yahwist), and so is Genesis 8:20-22. So the contradiction is internal to a single source, not just an artifact of redaction. Robert Alter handles this by reading the divine character development across the narrative — God learns that destruction doesn't fix the human condition and resolves on a different strategy. That's a literary reading and it has real merit, but it concedes that God in Genesis 8:21 is not the immutable God of later systematic theology. He's a deity who changes his mind in response to experience. Either the deity learns and changes (which contradicts immutability) or the text contradicts itself about the relationship between human evil and divine destruction. Take your pick.

answers.answer_explanation: And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake; for the imagination of man's heart [is] evil from his youth; neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done.

commentary_out.commentary:
This is among the cleaner contradictions in the primeval history, because the same Hebrew clause anchors two opposite divine resolutions. In Genesis 6:5 the LORD sees that "every imagination (Hebrew *yetser*) of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (*kol-yetser mahshevot libbo raq ra*), and in consequence resolves to wipe out humanity. In Genesis 8:21, after the flood, the LORD declares he will never again curse the ground or smite every living thing, and gives as his reason "for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth" (*ki yetser lev ha-adam ra mineurav*). The same evil *yetser* of the heart functions as the explicit grounds — the *ki*, "because" — for opposite decisions: destruction in chapter 6, forbearance in chapter 8.

The most common harmonization, run by Kenneth Mathews in the NAC and in modified form by Gordon Wenham, reads 8:21 as God's mercy responding to Noah's sacrifice (8:20-21 opens with the LORD smelling the "sweet savour"). On this account the post-flood promise is a new covenantal disposition; circumstances have changed, so the two passages address different moments and do not strictly contradict. This works as narrative sequence, but it does not dissolve the contradiction in the stated reasoning, because the text does not ground the restraint in the sacrifice. The causal clause is explicit and it is about the human heart: God withholds future destruction *because* man's inclination is evil from youth. The very datum that triggered judgment now triggers patience.

This is also one of the standard exhibits for source-critical analysis of the flood narrative. Hermann Gunkel, Claus Westermann, and more recently Joel Baden assign both Genesis 6:5-8 and Genesis 8:20-22 to J, the Yahwist, who frames the flood with these two heart-of-man oracles. That assignment matters: the contradiction is internal to a single source, not merely an artifact of the documentary interweaving (the P strand contributes the covenant and the more legal material). Westermann reads the J frame etiologically — the narrative explains why, despite persistent human wickedness, the cosmic order is now stable: God has resolved, once and for all, not to respond to that wickedness with annihilation. On this literary reading the repetition of the *yetser* clause is deliberate, marking a shift in divine policy, not a logical slip.

Robert Alter presses the literary point into a reading of divine character: across the narrative God appears to learn that destruction does not cure the human condition and so adopts a different strategy of forbearance and covenant. The reading has real merit and is faithful to the narrative's contours. But it concedes precisely what later systematic theology would resist: the God of Genesis 8:21, like the God of 6:6 who "repented" (Hebrew *naham*) that he had made humankind, is a deity who changes his mind in response to experience. That collides with doctrines of divine immutability and exhaustive foreknowledge — if God knew the human heart would remain evil, the flood resolved nothing he did not already know, and the post-flood promise reads as a course correction.

The horns are therefore clear. Either God's policy toward human evil genuinely changed between chapter 6 and chapter 8 (which the J narrative seems to depict, at the cost of immutability), or the same source has juxtaposed two incompatible inferences from the identical premise. The Noah-sacrifice harmonization rescues the narrative flow but cannot erase the fact that the text itself names the evil heart, not the sacrifice, as the reason for restraint. Verdict: genuine contradiction in the stated divine reasoning, internal to the Yahwist source.

entries.question: Did Jesus teach physical resistance?
entries.summary: Matthew 5:39 has Jesus teaching non-resistance: do not resist evil, turn the other cheek. Matthew 26:52 has him telling Peter to put away his sword because those who take the sword perish by it. But Luke 22:36 has Jesus instructing his disciples to sell their cloaks and buy swords, and John 2:15 has Jesus himself making a whip of cords and physically driving moneychangers out of the temple. The Jesus of the Sermon on the Mount and the Jesus of the temple cleansing don't appear to operate on the same ethic.
entries.commentary: The apologetic harmonizations on this one are unusually creative because the surface contradiction is so visible. For Luke 22:36 — "he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one" — Joel Green in the NICNT Luke and others read it as ironic or symbolic. Jesus is telling them to gear up rhetorically for opposition, not to literally arm themselves, which is why two swords (Luke 22:38) is somehow enough. The problem is that two swords being "enough" only makes sense if the swords are literal, just sufficient for a small defensive band. If the swords were purely symbolic, the disciples wouldn't have presented physical weapons. For John 2:15 — the temple cleansing — apologists often argue that the whip was only used on the animals, not the people. The Greek is genuinely ambiguous (*pantas exebalen* — "he drove them all out" — with *ta te probata kai tous boas* clarifying "both the sheep and the oxen"). D. A. Carson in the Pillar John commentary argues the whip targeted livestock, not humans. But the action is still physical force, and "drove them all out" most naturally includes the merchants. Raymond Brown in the Anchor Bible John takes the violence as directed at moneychangers and merchants, not just animals. So even on the most charitable reading, Jesus uses physical force to expel humans from a religious space. The non-resistance teaching in Matthew 5:39 is also widely understood by critical scholars (Dale Allison, John Meier) as referring to personal honor-disputes — slaps to the face are insults, not lethal attacks — rather than a comprehensive pacifism. So both ends of the contradiction get qualified: the resistance teaching may be narrower than absolute pacifism, and the swords/whip incidents may be narrower than general endorsements of violence. But the contradiction persists. The Sermon on the Mount Jesus and the temple-cleansing Jesus represent two streams of tradition about how Jesus related to coercive force, and the harmonizations work only if you let each text qualify the other rather than letting either stand at full strength.

commentary_out.commentary:
Two portraits of Jesus' relation to coercive force sit in visible tension. Matthew 5:39 teaches non-resistance — "resist not evil" (*mē antistēnai tō ponērō*), turn the other cheek — and Matthew 26:52 has Jesus rebuke armed defense at his arrest: "all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." Against these, Luke 22:36 has Jesus tell the disciples to sell a garment and buy a sword, and John 2:15 shows Jesus making a whip of cords and driving the temple traders out by force. The Sermon-on-the-Mount Jesus and the temple-cleansing Jesus do not obviously share an ethic of force.

The harmonizations are ingenious. For Luke 22:36, Joel Green and others read the sword saying as ironic or symbolic — Jesus signals that a season of hostility and rejection is coming (fulfilling Isaiah 53:12, "reckoned among the transgressors," which Luke quotes in 22:37), not that the disciples should arm for combat. The decisive internal clue is that when the disciples produce two swords, Jesus says "It is enough" (Luke 22:38, *hikanon estin*) — and two swords are absurdly insufficient for any real fight, which many read as Jesus breaking off a conversation the disciples have misunderstood. Yet the same datum cuts the other way: the swords presented are literal physical weapons, and at the arrest one disciple actually strikes with one (Luke 22:49-50; cf. all four Gospels), so the tradition plainly remembers armed followers. Whatever Luke intends rhetorically, the historical residue is a Jesus movement that carried weapons.

For John 2:15 the favored move limits the whip to the animals. The Greek is genuinely ambiguous: *kai pantas exebalen ek tou hierou ta te probata kai tous boas* — "and he drove them all out of the temple, both the sheep and the oxen." Defenders such as D. A. Carson argue *pantas* (masculine plural, "all") is then specified by "the sheep and the oxen," so the whip targeted livestock. But *pantas* is masculine while *probata* (sheep) is neuter, which makes a reference limited strictly to animals grammatically strained; the more natural antecedent of "all" includes the people. Raymond Brown takes the action as directed at the merchants and moneychangers, whose tables Jesus overturns and whose coins he scatters — acts of force against persons and property, not against sheep. Even the most charitable reading concedes Jesus used physical coercion to clear a religious space.

Both poles of the contradiction also need qualifying, which narrows but does not close the gap. Matthew 5:39's "resist not evil" is widely read by critical scholars (Dale Allison, John Meier) within an honor-culture frame: a blow to the right cheek is a backhanded insult, not a lethal assault, so the saying addresses retaliation in personal honor-disputes rather than legislating absolute pacifism. And the sword and whip episodes are situational, not programmatic endorsements of violence. So the resistance teaching may be narrower than pacifism, and the force episodes narrower than a doctrine of force.

Still, the tension is real and arguably reflects two streams of tradition and two communities' concerns. Mark frames Jesus' movement against the live question of armed revolt — one of the Twelve is "Simon the Zealot," Barabbas is a violent insurrectionist released in Jesus' place, and Jesus is crucified between *lēstai* (a term Josephus uses for bandit-rebels) under a charge of sedition. The Gospels work hard to present Jesus as non-seditious while preserving memories — armed disciples, a forcible temple demonstration — that point the other way. The non-resistance sayings likely reflect later ecclesial articulation of an ethic for a vulnerable community; the sword and whip episodes preserve harder, less domesticated tradition. The harmonization succeeds only by letting each text qualify the other until neither stands at full strength. Verdict: genuine tension between two tradition-streams, only partially harmonizable.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Matthew 5:39 likely addresses honor-disputes (a backhand insult) rather than absolute pacifism, and the Luke 22:36 sword saying and John 2:15 cleansing are situational rather than programmatic; but the texts still preserve a Jesus who carried armed followers and used physical force, so the ethic is reconciled only by mutually narrowing each pole — leaving a real residual tension between tradition-streams.

entries.question: Should you be baptized?
entries.summary: Matthew 28:19 places baptism at the center of the risen Jesus' Great Commission to the eleven — go, make disciples, baptize them in the triune name. Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:14, 17 says the opposite about his own mission — he thanks God he baptized almost no one in Corinth, and flatly states that Christ did not send him to baptize but to preach the gospel. The contradiction is at the level of mission priority: Matthew's Jesus makes baptism constitutive of the commission; Paul explicitly excludes it from his own.
entries.commentary: The tension here is real but more nuanced than a flat yes/no contradiction. Matthew 28:19 is the climactic command of the Gospel — disciples are made by baptizing and teaching, in the triune name. Most critical scholars (Davies-Allison, Luz) treat 28:19 as a late, post-resurrection composition reflecting the practice of Matthew's community c. 80-90 CE, including the developed triune baptismal formula which is otherwise unattested in this form in the rest of the NT. Paul, writing earlier (mid-50s CE) and apparently unaware of any dominical baptismal command, treats baptism as ancillary to his apostolic calling. In 1 Corinthians 1:17 he draws a sharp distinction: "Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel." Apologists like Blomberg harmonize by noting that Paul baptized *some* (Crispus, Gaius, the household of Stephanas) and that his statement is hyperbolic emphasis on preaching, not rejection of the rite. Fair enough — but that harmonization assumes Paul knew of and accepted the Great Commission as a binding command, which the textual evidence doesn't support. If Paul had received a dominical instruction to baptize all nations, his rhetorical disavowal in 1 Corinthians 1:17 would be theologically suicidal. The more parsimonious reading is that the Great Commission in its Matthean form represents a later ecclesiastical development that Paul did not inherit. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence, but the evidence leans heavily in that direction.

For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect.

commentary_out.commentary:
Matthew 28:19 makes baptism constitutive of the church's foundational mission: the risen Jesus commissions the eleven to "make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Paul, in 1 Corinthians 1:14-17, appears to push in the opposite direction: he thanks God he baptized almost no one at Corinth (only Crispus, Gaius, and the household of Stephanas, which he adds as an afterthought in v. 16), and concludes, "For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel." Read flatly, Matthew's Jesus centers the rite while Paul marginalizes it.

Several features sharpen and several soften the tension. On the sharpening side, the triadic baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 is unattested in this developed form anywhere else in the New Testament. Acts uniformly reports baptism "in the name of Jesus" or "of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5), and Paul likewise knows only baptism "into Christ" (Rom 6:3; Gal 3:27). The earliest extra-canonical witness, Didache 7, contains the triune formula but also preserves the older single-name practice in Didache 9:5, suggesting the trinitarian wording was crystallizing in the late first or early second century — the period most critical scholars (Davies-Allison, Luz) assign to Matthew's final form, c. 80-90 CE. The Matthean commission, on this analysis, reflects the liturgy of Matthew's community projected back onto the lips of the risen Jesus, a standard feature of post-resurrection appearance narratives.

On the softening side, the harmonization defended by Blomberg is genuinely strong and should not be caricatured. Paul did baptize; he simply did not regard administering the rite personally as the heart of his commission. His statement in 1 Corinthians 1:17 is occasioned by a specific pastoral problem — the Corinthians were forming personality cults around the persons who baptized them ("I am of Paul; and I of Apollos," 1:12), and Paul deliberately distances himself from baptism precisely to deflate those factions. The verb "sent" (apesteilen) places the remark within Paul's division of apostolic labor, not within a theology that rejects the sacrament. Indeed Paul's most sustained theological statement on baptism, Romans 6:3-4, treats it as the believer's incorporation into Christ's death and resurrection — hardly the language of a man who thinks baptism dispensable. So at the level of practice and theology of the rite, the two texts are reconcilable: both presuppose baptism; they differ on emphasis, and the difference is explained by Paul's polemical setting (Fitzmyer, Conzelmann).

The residual, irreducible tension is narrower but real. If Paul had received and accepted a dominical command obliging him to baptize all nations, the rhetorical disavowal of 1 Corinthians 1:17 would be a strange way to argue, since it sets his own sending against a command of the risen Lord. The more economical reading is that Paul wrote in the mid-50s without knowledge of the Great Commission in its Matthean form, which represents a later development of the tradition (Ehrman). That conclusion is an inference from silence and remains a judgment about probabilities rather than a demonstration. Verdict: largely harmonizable at the level of mission and practice (hyperbole plus differing emphasis), with a genuine but narrower historical tension over whether the Matthean baptismal command was known to Paul.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: At the level of whether baptism is practiced, the two are reconcilable: Paul did baptize (1 Cor 1:14-16) and presupposes baptism as foundational (Rom 6:3-4); his 1 Cor 1:17 is rhetorical hyperbole subordinating baptism to preaching within his own division of apostolic labor, not a denial of the rite. The residual tension is at the level of whether a dominical command to baptize all nations was known to Paul.

entries.question: Is it okay to marry your brother's widow?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 25:5 not only permits but commands a man to marry his deceased brother's childless widow — the institution of levirate marriage (Hebrew yibbum), with the explicit purpose of raising up offspring to perpetuate the dead brother's name. Leviticus 20:21 flatly prohibits exactly the same act, calling it an "unclean thing" (niddah) that uncovers the brother's nakedness, with the penalty that the couple shall be childless. Same action, opposite rulings.
entries.commentary: This is one of the cleanest Pentateuchal legal contradictions in the entire corpus, and it's been recognized as such since the medieval rabbis. The Levitical prohibition (Holiness Code, H source) treats marriage to a brother's wife as incest — the same logic that prohibits a man from "uncovering the nakedness" of his father's wife or his daughter-in-law. The penalty in Leviticus 20:21 is even thematically barbed: the violators will be childless, which is precisely the opposite outcome from what Deuteronomy 25 commands the levirate to *prevent*. The Deuteronomic law (D source) addresses a different social anxiety entirely — preserving the dead man's lineage and inheritance line. Apologists like Archer and Walton harmonize by claiming Leviticus addresses marriage to a living brother's wife (adultery) while Deuteronomy addresses marriage to a deceased brother's widow. That harmonization is textually plausible for Leviticus 18:16 (which is parallel), but it strains Leviticus 20:21, which doesn't specify the brother's state. More importantly, the rabbinic tradition itself acknowledged the tension — m. Yebamot is one giant attempt to harmonize the laws, ultimately concluding that the Deuteronomic levirate *overrides* the Levitical prohibition only in the specific case of childless widowhood. That's not harmonization; that's legislative arbitration between two laws that conflict on their face. Source criticism explains this cleanly: H and D reflect distinct legal traditions with different priorities — H is preoccupied with priestly purity, D with social and economic preservation of the family line.

commentary_out.commentary:
Deuteronomy 25:5-10 commands levirate marriage (Hebrew yibbum): when brothers dwell together and one dies childless, the surviving brother "shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife," so that the firstborn "shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel." Leviticus 20:21 declares the seemingly identical act forbidden: "if a man shall take his brother's wife, it is an unclean thing (niddah); he hath uncovered his brother's nakedness; they shall be childless." The Hebrew niddah ordinarily denotes menstrual impurity and by extension abhorrent defilement, and the prescribed consequence — childlessness ("riyriym, 'stripped/childless') — is thematically barbed: it is the precise outcome the Deuteronomic levirate exists to prevent.

The most natural source-critical placement is that Leviticus 20:21 belongs to the Holiness Code (H, Lev 17-26), whose incest catalogue in Leviticus 18 prohibits "uncovering the nakedness" of a long list of kin defined through a male relative — father's wife, daughter-in-law, and at 18:16 "thy brother's wife." H's logic is genealogical and cultic: such unions defile the land. Deuteronomy 25 (D) operates from a different concern — the preservation of the dead man's name, line, and property within the patrimony. Two legal traditions, two priorities, one act.

The strongest harmonization, defended by Archer and by John Walton, restricts the Levitical prohibition to a brother's wife while the brother is alive, making it a prohibition of adultery and incest within a living union, and reserves Deuteronomy 25 for the widow of a brother who has died childless. This reading has real support: Leviticus 18:16's parallel sits in a list otherwise concerned with relations that would constitute adultery or rivalry within the extended household, and Jacob Milgrom argues that 18:16 indeed contemplates the wife of a living brother. The reading thus resolves the parallel at 18:16 cleanly. The difficulty is that Leviticus 20:21 itself does not specify the brother's state, and its penalty clause (childlessness) is most pointed precisely if the union in view is one undertaken after a brother's death to produce children — which is exactly the levirate situation. If H simply meant adultery with a living brother's wife, the death penalty applied elsewhere in the chapter to adultery (Lev 20:10) would be expected, not the distinctive sentence of childlessness.

The rabbinic tradition itself conceded a real conflict and resolved it by legislative arbitration rather than by claiming the laws never overlapped. The Mishnah's entire tractate Yebamot is devoted to defining when the Deuteronomic levirate obligation overrides the general Levitical prohibition of a brother's wife, concluding that the mitzvah of yibbum suspends the prohibition only in the precise case of a childless widow, and that outside that case the prohibition stands with full force. That is not the harmony of two laws that never touched; it is a ruling about which of two genuinely competing statutes prevails in a defined situation. The narrative tradition assumes levirate duty as normative and praiseworthy — Genesis 38 (Tamar, Judah, and the failure of Onan) and the book of Ruth both turn on the obligation to raise up seed for a dead kinsman. Verdict: a real legal tension between H and D that the case-distinction harmonization can partly but not fully dissolve; the rabbis themselves treated it as a conflict requiring one law to override the other.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The texts can be read as addressing different cases if Leviticus is restricted to a brother's wife during the brother's lifetime (adultery/incest with a living brother's spouse) while Deuteronomy governs the childless widow of a deceased brother. This is the rabbinic resolution. The harmonization is plausible for the parallel Lev 18:16 but strained for Lev 20:21, which does not specify the brother's state and whose penalty (childlessness) is thematically the inverse of the levirate's purpose.

issues.problem: The commentary glosses the childlessness penalty term as '"riyriym, stripped/childless".' The Hebrew of Leviticus 20:21 is 'aririm yihyu' (עֲרִירִים יִהְיוּ), 'they shall be childless,' from the root meaning stripped/childless. The transliteration 'riyriym' is garbled/incorrect — it drops the initial ayin and misrepresents the word. A stated Hebrew form that is malformed is a language error.
